title: Service-to-Service Authentication: mTLS and Workload Identity
objectives: Explain why network location is not an identity
Describe what mutual TLS proves and what it leaves to authorisation
Design short-lived, automatically rotated workload certificates

cards.title: Being inside the network is not an identity
cards.body: Many systems trust any request that comes from an internal address. Then one compromised container, laptop on the VPN or misrouted load balancer can call every internal service. Zero trust, as NIST SP 800-207 describes it, removes that implicit trust: each request is authenticated and authorised on its own, wherever it comes from. Firewalls and private subnets still help, but they limit where traffic can reach. They do not prove who sent it.

cards.title: Mutual TLS: both sides show a certificate
cards.body: In ordinary TLS only the server proves who it is. In mutual TLS (mTLS) the server also asks for a client certificate, and the client proves it holds the matching private key during the handshake. The receiver checks that the certificate chains to a CA it trusts for workloads. It then reads the identity from the certificate, usually a URI such as spiffe://prod/ns/payments/sa/api in the subject alternative name. That identity becomes the input to an access policy.

cards.title: Worked example: payments calls the ledger
cards.body: The payments service must create ledger entries. Nothing else may.
steps: The platform verifies the payments workload (which cluster, namespace and service account it runs as) and issues a 24-hour certificate naming it
Payments opens TLS to the ledger and checks the ledger’s certificate chains to the internal CA and names the ledger
The ledger asks for a client certificate, verifies the chain and the key proof, and reads the identity spiffe://prod/ns/payments/sa/api
The ledger’s policy allows that identity to POST /entries and nothing else; every other identity gets 403
Payments renews at about half the lifetime, so a failed renewal leaves 12 hours to fix it before anything breaks

cards.title: Misconception: mTLS is authorisation
cards.body: mTLS answers “which workload is calling?” It does not answer “may it do this?”. A ledger that accepts any certificate from the internal CA still lets a compromised reporting service write entries. Pair mTLS with a per-endpoint policy keyed on the workload identity. The certificate also names the service, not the customer. When the end user matters, pass their identity separately as a signed, short-lived token, and check both.

cards.title: Trap: long-lived certificates nobody rotates
cards.body: A two-year certificate installed by hand fails twice. Its private key stays useful to a thief for months, and one day it expires and takes the service down because nobody remembered. Short lifetimes (hours to days) with automatic issuance and renewal fix both. Alert when any certificate is within a quarter of its lifetime of expiry and has not renewed. Keep the CA’s own key in a KMS or HSM, because whoever holds it can mint any identity.

questions.prompt: An attacker gets code running in one container of a cluster whose services trust any request from an internal address. What can it most likely do?

choices.label: Call internal services as if it were any trusted caller
Little, because internal traffic is already encrypted with TLS
Read only the files of the container it compromised
Reach the internet but none of the internal services

questions.explanation: Trust based on source address means any foothold inside inherits that trust. Encryption hides traffic from eavesdroppers but does not authenticate the sender. A foothold is not confined to its own files when the network itself grants access, and egress rules do not stop east-west calls.

questions.prompt: In mutual TLS, what does the server learn that ordinary TLS does not tell it?

choices.label: That the connection is encrypted in both directions
The client’s identity, proven with its private key
Which end user is behind the calling service
That the client’s code has not been modified

questions.explanation: The extra step is the client certificate and the proof of its private key. Ordinary TLS already encrypts both directions. The certificate names the workload, not the end user, and it says nothing about whether the workload’s code was tampered with.

questions.prompt: The ledger accepts mTLS from any certificate signed by the internal workload CA. What is still missing?

choices.label: A second handshake for each request
Longer RSA keys in each workload certificate
Rules for which identities may call which endpoints
Encryption of the request body inside the TLS tunnel

questions.explanation: Authentication without authorisation lets every workload with a certificate call every endpoint. Extra handshakes, bigger keys and body encryption add cost but still let a compromised service make calls it should not.

questions.prompt: A fleet of 2,000 workloads uses 24-hour certificates, each renewed at half its lifetime. How many certificates does the CA issue per hour?
questions.workedAnswer: Each workload renews every 12 hours, so 2,000 / 12 ≈ 167 issuances per hour, about 4,000 a day.
questions.explanation: Design implication: renewing at half life doubles issuance compared with renewing at expiry (83 per hour), but leaves time to recover from a failed renewal.

questions.prompt: Order how a workload gets and uses its identity.

items.label: The workload presents it in an mTLS handshake
The platform verifies where the workload runs (attestation)
The workload renews the certificate before it expires
The platform issues a short-lived certificate naming the workload
The receiver checks the chain and maps the identity to a policy

questions.explanation: Identity is issued only after the platform has checked what the workload is. It is then used and checked, and renewed before expiry.

questions.prompt: Renewal is automated either way. Why prefer 24-hour service certificates over 2-year ones?

choices.label: Short certificates make each handshake faster
Clients refuse internal certificates older than a day
Revocation lists only work for short certificates
A stolen private key stops being useful within a day

questions.explanation: Short lifetimes limit how long a stolen key works without relying on revocation, which clients often check poorly. Handshake speed does not depend on lifetime. No client rule rejects day-old certificates, and revocation lists apply to any lifetime.

flashcards.back: Implicit trust based on network location: each request is authenticated and authorised.

flashcards.front: What extra thing does mTLS prove?
flashcards.back: The client holds the private key for a certificate naming its identity.
A stolen key expires quickly, and automated renewal is exercised all the time.

mechanism.title: How workload identity works end to end
steps: Attest: before issuing anything, the platform checks facts it controls, such as the node, the cluster, the namespace and the service account. Do not trust anything the workload merely claims about itself.

Issue: a workload CA signs a short-lived certificate whose subject alternative name carries a structured identity (for example a SPIFFE ID). The private key is generated on the workload and never leaves it.

Authenticate: every connection uses mTLS. Each side checks the peer’s chain against the workload trust bundle and reads the peer identity. A sidecar proxy or a library can do this so application code stays simple.
Authorise: a policy maps caller identity to allowed operations, such as payments may POST /entries on the ledger. Deny by default, and keep policies in version control with review.

Propagate the user: when a request acts for a customer, forward a signed, short-lived user token alongside the service identity. The receiver checks both: is this service allowed, and is this user allowed?
Rotate and observe: renew at about half the lifetime, alert on renewal failures and near-expiry certificates, and log the caller identity for every denied request.

useWhen: Many services call each other inside a cluster or across clouds
Compliance or a past incident demands proof of which service made each call
avoidWhen: A single service with one database and no internal callers, where the cost outweighs the gain
Calls from customers’ browsers, which should use user tokens rather than client certificates

rows: Any foothold inside inherits the trust
Keys leak, rarely rotate and are copied between services
Which workload holds the private key
Needs a CA, rotation and an authorisation policy
Which service the issuer vouched for
Bearer token: replayable until it expires unless bound to the connection

numbers.title: What short lifetimes cost the CA
assumptions: About 5 ms of CA signing time per certificate (illustrative)
steps: Issuance: 2,000 × 2 renewals a day = 4,000 certificates a day, or about 167 an hour
Signing load: 4,000 × 5 ms = 20 seconds of CA work per day, which is negligible
Exposure: a stolen key works for at most 24 hours, against up to 730 days for a 2-year certificate
Failure budget: renewing at half life leaves 12 hours to notice and fix a broken renewal before outages start
numbers.result: The CA load is trivial, and the window in which a stolen key is useful shrinks by a factor of about 700.

india.title: NIST SP 800-207 tenets of zero trust
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust Architecture, 2020) lists tenets that match this design. All communication is secured regardless of network location. Access to each resource is granted per session. Access is decided by dynamic policy that includes the identity of the requester. Authentication and authorisation are dynamic and strictly enforced before access is allowed. Google’s BeyondProd paper describes the same idea applied to its own production services: mutual authentication between services, and service identity in place of network location.

pitfalls.trap: Accepting any certificate from the internal CA as permission to call anything
pitfalls.say: mTLS tells me who is calling. A deny-by-default policy per endpoint tells me whether they may.

pitfalls.trap: Hand-installed certificates with multi-year lifetimes
pitfalls.say: Automate issuance and renew at half life, so expiry is routine instead of an outage.

pitfalls.trap: Dropping the end user’s identity at the first internal hop
pitfalls.say: Forward a signed user token so downstream services can still enforce per-customer rules.

takeaways: Network location limits reach; it does not prove identity
mTLS proves which workload holds a key, and a policy decides what it may do
Short-lived, automatically renewed certificates shrink the value of a stolen key
Carry the end user’s identity separately from the service identity

interactive.title: Who gets in?
interactive.prompt: The ledger requires mTLS from the internal CA, and its policy lets only the payments identity POST /entries. An attacker controls the reports service, which has a valid certificate for its own identity.

choices.label: Reports connects, but POST /entries is refused by policy
choices.feedback: Right: authentication succeeds and authorisation denies it.

choices.label: Reports can post entries because its certificate is valid
choices.feedback: A valid certificate only says who it is; the policy does not list reports.

choices.label: Reports can post entries after copying the payments certificate
choices.feedback: The certificate is public. Without the payments private key the handshake fails.

interactive.reveal: Identity plus a deny-by-default policy contains a compromised service to what it was already allowed to do.

seeAlso.why: The TLS handshake that mTLS extends with a client certificate
Secrets managers issue short-lived credentials using the same workload identity
Private networking limits reach, which complements identity checks

title: Encryption at Rest and Envelope Encryption
objectives: Say what storage encryption protects against and what it does not
Explain envelope encryption with data keys and a KMS
Plan key rotation and crypto-shredding without re-encrypting everything

cards.title: What encryption at rest protects, and what it does not
cards.body: Disk, volume and database storage encryption protect against someone who gets the bytes without going through your system. Examples are a stolen or discarded drive, a snapshot shared to the wrong account, or a backup tape left in a taxi. They do not protect against an attacker who queries through the application or holds its database credentials. The storage layer decrypts for every authorised read, so it decrypts for them too. To protect a field from people with database access, encrypt it in the application with a key the database cannot use.

cards.title: Envelope encryption: a key for the data, a key for the key
cards.body: Generate a random data key (DEK), encrypt the data locally with an AEAD cipher such as AES-256-GCM, then ask the key management service (KMS) to encrypt the DEK under a key-encryption key (KEK) that never leaves the KMS. Store the wrapped DEK next to the ciphertext. To read, send the wrapped DEK to the KMS, get the plaintext DEK back and decrypt locally. Bulk data never crosses the network to the KMS. That matters because KMS calls take small inputs: AWS KMS Encrypt accepts up to 4,096 bytes, and Cloud KMS up to 64 KiB.

cards.title: Worked example: encrypting a 2 GB backup
cards.body: A nightly database backup must be unreadable to anyone who copies the file but lacks KMS permission.
steps: Ask the KMS for a new 256-bit data key; it returns the key in plain form and wrapped under the backup KEK
Encrypt the backup locally in chunks with AES-256-GCM, using a unique nonce for each chunk
Write the wrapped data key, a few hundred bytes, into the backup header
Erase the plain data key from memory once the backup is written
To restore, the KMS unwraps the key only after checking the caller’s permission, and it logs the call

cards.title: Misconception: rotating the master key means re-encrypting all data
cards.body: When a KMS rotates a KEK, it creates a new key version and keeps the old versions to unwrap DEKs they protected. New DEKs are wrapped under the new version. Optionally you re-wrap old DEKs, which means rewriting a few hundred bytes per object, not the object itself. Re-encrypting the data is needed only when a DEK itself may have been exposed. Rotation therefore limits how much data any one key version protects, at almost no cost.

cards.title: Trap: the key stored next to the data
cards.body: Encrypting a column while keeping the key in the same database, or in a config file in the repository, means one leak hands over both. Keep KEKs in a KMS or HSM with an access policy separate from the data’s, and audit every unwrap. The reverse danger is just as real: deleting a KEK destroys every DEK it wrapped. KMSs make you schedule deletion with a waiting period (AWS KMS: 7 to 30 days) so a mistake can be cancelled.

questions.prompt: The cloud provider encrypts a database volume at rest. An attacker steals the app’s database password. What does the volume encryption do for you?

choices.label: It blocks the queries, since the attacker lacks the disk key
Little: the database decrypts rows for any valid login
It returns rows still encrypted, so they are unreadable
It forces a second login using the KMS key

questions.explanation: Storage encryption is transparent to authorised readers. A valid database login is an authorised reader, so the queries succeed and return plain rows. The disk key is used by the storage layer, not requested from clients, and the KMS is not involved in each SQL login.

questions.prompt: Why encrypt a 2 GB file with a local data key instead of sending the file to the KMS?

choices.label: A local key is stronger than a key held in the KMS
Local encryption removes the need to store any key
KMS calls take small inputs, and bulk data stays local
The data key can then be stored unwrapped beside the file

questions.explanation: KMS encrypt calls are limited to kilobytes, and shipping gigabytes to a central service would be slow and costly. Key strength is the same, since both are 256-bit. You still store the data key, but wrapped by the KMS, never unwrapped next to the data.

questions.prompt: The KMS rotates its master key every year. What happens to data encrypted three years ago?

choices.label: It must be re-encrypted before the rotation can finish
It becomes unreadable, which is the point of rotating
It stays readable, since old key versions unwrap old data keys
It is quietly re-encrypted in place by the storage layer

questions.explanation: Rotation adds a version and keeps the old ones for decryption. Nothing is re-encrypted unless you choose to re-wrap the data keys. Making old data unreadable is what key deletion does, not rotation.

questions.prompt: Each customer’s records are encrypted under that customer’s own data key. One customer asks to be erased, but copies sit in 40 backups. What does destroying their key do?

choices.label: Makes their records in all 40 backups unreadable
Shrinks the backups by removing their records
Has no effect until each backup is restored and edited
Also destroys other customers’ data in those backups

questions.explanation: Crypto-shredding makes the ciphertext useless wherever it is, without touching the backups. The bytes are still there, so the backups do not shrink. Other customers use different keys and are unaffected.

questions.prompt: A service writes 50 million objects a day and requests a new data key from the KMS for each. On average, how many KMS calls per second is that?
questions.workedAnswer: 50,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 579 calls per second on average, and peaks will be higher.
questions.explanation: Design implication: that load can approach a provider’s request quotas, so batch objects under one data key or cache data keys briefly with strict limits.

questions.prompt: Order a read of an envelope-encrypted record.

items.label: Decrypt the record locally with the returned data key
Send the wrapped data key to the KMS
Erase the plain data key from memory
Load the ciphertext and its wrapped data key
The KMS checks the caller’s permission and logs the request

questions.explanation: The KMS sees only the small wrapped key and decides whether to unwrap it. The bulk decryption happens locally.

flashcards.front: What does disk encryption not stop?
flashcards.back: Anyone who reads through the application or with valid database credentials.
Encrypt data with a local data key; encrypt that key under a KMS key that never leaves the KMS.
Destroying a key so every copy of the data it protected becomes unreadable.

Google Cloud KMS: Envelope encryption
OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5: Key Management

mechanism.title: Layers of encryption at rest and how keys flow
steps: Choose the threat first. Storage encryption covers lost media and stray snapshots. Application-level (field) encryption also covers database administrators, SQL injection that reads raw columns, and leaked database credentials, because the database never holds the key.

Generate a fresh data key per object, per file or per tenant, using the KMS or a CSPRNG. Encrypt with an AEAD cipher and a unique nonce, and bind context (such as the record id) as associated data so ciphertext cannot be swapped between rows.
Wrap the data key under a KEK in the KMS. The KEK’s access policy names which workloads may unwrap, and every unwrap is logged, which gives you an audit trail of who read what.
Rotate KEKs on a schedule. The KMS keeps old versions for unwrapping, so rotation is cheap. Re-wrap DEKs if policy requires, and re-encrypt data only if a DEK was exposed.
Choose the key granularity on purpose. One DEK per customer enables crypto-shredding: destroying it erases that customer’s data everywhere, including in backups you cannot edit.

Plan for KMS outages and costs. Cache unwrapped DEKs in memory for minutes, with a cap on how many objects each may encrypt. Treat KEK deletion as a destructive change: disable first, watch for failures, and only then schedule deletion.

useWhen: Data with legal or contractual protection, or held for many tenants
You need per-customer erasure that reaches backups
avoidWhen: Public or easily regenerated data, where key management adds risk without benefit
You would have to keep the KEK beside the data, which adds complexity without separation

rows: Anyone reading through the database or app
Database admins and leaked DB credentials
A compromised app server that can unwrap keys
The whole server side, including the operator
Lost keys, and features such as server-side search

numbers.title: KMS calls for 50 million objects a day
assumptions: One data key per object, or one per batch of 1,000 objects
Peak traffic about 3 times the average (illustrative)
steps: Per object: 50,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 579 calls per second to KMS, on average
At a 3× peak that is about 1,740 calls per second, which can hit request quotas and adds a network round trip to every write
Per batch of 1,000: 579 / 1,000 ≈ 0.58 calls per second, about 50,000 calls a day
Trade-off: one key then protects 1,000 objects, so crypto-shredding a single object is no longer possible
numbers.result: Batching data keys cuts KMS traffic about 1,000-fold. Pick the batch boundary to match what you may need to erase on its own, such as one customer.

india.title: AWS KMS and Google Cloud KMS on envelope encryption
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The AWS KMS documentation defines envelope encryption as encrypting plaintext with a data key and then encrypting the data key under another key. Its Encrypt operation accepts at most 4,096 bytes with a symmetric key, which is why bulk data is encrypted locally. Google Cloud’s guidance says Cloud KMS was designed to manage key-encryption keys, so its Encrypt and Decrypt input is capped at 64 KiB. It recommends generating data keys locally and storing them wrapped next to the data they protect. AWS requires a waiting period of 7 to 30 days before a KMS key is actually deleted.

pitfalls.trap: Claiming the database is safe because “it is encrypted at rest”
pitfalls.say: Storage encryption covers lost media. For people with database access I need field encryption with a key the database cannot use.

pitfalls.trap: Deleting an old KMS key to tidy up
pitfalls.say: Disable it first and watch for failures; deletion destroys every data key it wrapped.

pitfalls.trap: Reusing a nonce with AES-GCM because the key is per object
pitfalls.say: A per-object key with a fresh random nonce per encryption avoids nonce reuse, which would break GCM.

takeaways: Storage encryption protects media, not data read through the system
Envelope encryption keeps bulk data local and keys in the KMS
KEK rotation is cheap because old versions keep unwrapping
Per-customer data keys make erasure reach backups through crypto-shredding

interactive.title: What does deleting the key do?
interactive.prompt: An engineer schedules deletion of the KMS key that wraps every data key for the orders database, thinking it is unused. The waiting period is 30 days.

choices.label: If nobody cancels, all order data becomes unreadable for good
choices.feedback: Right: every data key it wrapped can no longer be unwrapped.

choices.label: Orders stay readable, because the data keys are cached
choices.feedback: Caches expire within minutes; after that, nothing can unwrap the data keys.

choices.label: The KMS re-wraps the data keys under a default key
choices.feedback: No KMS does this. Deletion is final once the waiting period ends.

interactive.reveal: Disable the key first and alert on decryption failures during the waiting period; that turns a silent disaster into a cancelled change.

seeAlso.why: AEAD and key types underpin the data keys used here
Secrets managers and KMSs share the same access-policy and audit model
Backups need a key strategy, or a restore can fail when you need it

title: Defending Login: Credential Stuffing, Lockouts and Enumeration
objectives: Recognise credential stuffing and why per-IP limits miss it
Choose throttling and step-up challenges over hard lockouts
Remove account-enumeration leaks from login, sign-up and reset flows

cards.title: Credential stuffing replays passwords that work elsewhere
cards.body: People reuse passwords, and billions of username and password pairs from other sites’ breaches circulate. In credential stuffing an attacker replays those pairs against your login, usually one attempt per account, spread across thousands of IP addresses. Only a small fraction succeed. The figures here are illustrative: 0.5% of 10 million attempts is still 50,000 accounts taken over. Because each address and each account sees only a few attempts, limits keyed only on IP or only on account barely notice.

cards.title: Hard lockouts hand attackers a denial of service
cards.body: Locking an account for a day after five failures stops guessing against that account. It also lets anyone who knows a username lock its owner out, and a script can do that to every user. Prefer per-account throttling that grows the delay with each failure, then a step-up check such as a second factor or a bot challenge, plus a notification to the owner. NIST SP 800-63B-4 caps consecutive failed attempts on one account at 100 before stronger measures. That figure is a ceiling, not a target.

cards.title: Worked example: layered limits on one login endpoint
cards.body: A consumer app with 20 million accounts wants to slow attacks without locking out real users.
steps: Per source address or network: about 20 attempts per minute, which slows single noisy sources
Per account: after 5 failures add a growing delay or a challenge; after 100 consecutive failures require recovery
Across the site: watch the failure ratio, since a jump from 10% to 60% failed logins signals a stuffing run
On every new or changed password: reject ones found in breach corpuses, and force a reset for accounts whose current password is exposed
Offer MFA and passkeys, which make a correct password alone insufficient

cards.title: Misconception: “Wrong password” is a helpful message
cards.body: If the login says “No such user” for one input and “Wrong password” for another, it confirms which accounts exist. Status codes, redirects and response times leak the same thing. A server that skips the slow password hash for unknown users answers in milliseconds instead of a quarter of a second. Return one message and status, and hash a dummy password when the user is missing. Sign-up and reset leak too, so say “If an account exists, we have sent a link”.

cards.title: Trap: a CAPTCHA as the only defence
cards.body: Challenges raise the cost per attempt, but paid solving services and automation get through many of them cheaply. They also hurt accessibility, and they do nothing once the attacker holds a correct password. Use challenges as one layer, triggered by risk signals such as a new device, a burst of failures or a flagged network. Behind them, put MFA, breached-password checks and alerts on unusual success patterns.

questions.prompt: Failed logins jump to 400,000 an hour from 30,000 addresses. Each attempt pairs a different username with a different password, and about 0.5% succeed. What is happening?

choices.label: Credential stuffing with pairs leaked from another site
Password spraying: one common password tried on many accounts
Brute force: many guesses aimed at a single account
A broken password hash rejecting real users after a deploy

questions.explanation: Distinct username and password pairs with a small success rate are the signature of replayed breach data. Spraying reuses the same few passwords across accounts. Brute force concentrates on one account. A broken hash would make real users fail, not make strangers succeed.

questions.prompt: Why is “lock the account for 24 hours after 5 failures” risky for a public consumer app?

choices.label: Anyone who knows a username can lock its owner out
It lets attackers guess without limit once the lock ends
Locking an account resets its MFA enrolment
It slows the password hash for the other users

questions.explanation: The control punishes the account owner for an attacker’s actions, and it can be scripted across many usernames. Five guesses a day is a tight limit, not an unlimited one. Lockout state is unrelated to MFA enrolment and to hashing cost.

questions.prompt: Login answers in 5 ms for unknown usernames and in 250 ms for wrong passwords, with identical text. What leaks?

choices.label: The password hash, through the error text
Which usernames exist, through the timing
The salt, through the size of the response
Nothing useful, because the messages match

questions.explanation: Only known users go through the slow hash, so timing separates them. Hash a dummy password for unknown users. The text, size and salt are not exposed here; matching messages are not enough when timing differs.

questions.prompt: An attacker replays 10 million leaked pairs, and 0.5% are valid on your site (an illustrative rate). How many accounts are taken over if none use MFA?
questions.explanation: Design implication: small percentages of huge lists add up. MFA stops most of these takeovers, because a correct password alone is no longer enough.

questions.prompt: Order the responses as failed attempts pile up on one account.

items.label: Require a bot challenge or a second factor
Allow attempts at normal speed
Notify the owner and require recovery at the hard limit
Add a short delay that grows with each failure

questions.explanation: Escalate friction gradually, so real users who mistype are barely slowed while sustained guessing becomes expensive.

questions.prompt: When should a site check passwords against a list of breached passwords?

choices.label: When one is set or changed, and optionally at login
Once a year, by scanning the stored password hashes
Only after the owner reports the account hacked
Only for administrator accounts

questions.explanation: NIST requires checking new passwords against compromised lists. Checking at login lets you force a reset when a current password turns up in a new breach. Slow, salted hashes cannot be scanned in bulk, waiting for a report is too late, and stuffing targets ordinary users.

questions.prompt: A shopping app sees nightly stuffing runs from residential IP addresses. Support complains that the current lockout policy blocks real customers.
constraints: Attempts spread over tens of thousands of addresses
One or two attempts per account

approaches.label: Risk-based challenges, breached-password resets and optional MFA
Stricter per-IP limits of 5 attempts per hour
Lock each account after 2 failures

rationaleOptions.label: Distributed attempts slip under per-IP and per-account limits
Challenges only on risk keep friction low for real customers
Tighter IP limits stop attacks from residential addresses
Lockouts stop stuffing because each pair is tried once

rationaleConflicts.r3: Each address sends only a few attempts, and residential ranges are shared with real customers.
rationaleConflicts.r4: With one attempt per account a lockout never triggers, but it does lock out real users.

questions.explanation: Stuffing is distributed and low-and-slow, so defend with signals across the whole site and with factors beyond the password.

flashcards.back: Stuffing replays leaked pairs; spraying tries a few common passwords on many accounts.
They let anyone lock a known user out; throttle and step up instead.

flashcards.front: How do you stop timing enumeration?
flashcards.back: Same message and status, and hash a dummy password when the user does not exist.

mechanism.title: How a layered login defence works
steps: Measure first: record each attempt with account, source network, device signals and outcome. Without a failure-ratio baseline you cannot tell a stuffing run from a busy evening.
Rate-limit on several keys at once: source address, network block, account and the whole site. Each key catches a different attack shape, and none catches them all.

Escalate per account instead of locking. Add a growing delay, then a challenge or second factor, and notify the owner. Keep a hard ceiling (NIST: at most 100 consecutive failures) that leads to recovery, not a timed lock anyone can trigger.
Make responses uniform: the same message, status and similar timing for unknown users, wrong passwords and locked accounts. Apply the same rule to sign-up and password reset.

Check passwords against breach corpuses when they are set, and at login if you can do it privately (for example with a k-anonymity range query that sends only a hash prefix). Force a reset when a match appears.
Remove the password’s value: offer MFA and passkeys, and prompt users towards them after a risky login. A replayed password then fails at the second step.

useWhen: Any public login, sign-up or reset endpoint
Apps where accounts hold money, loyalty points or personal data worth reselling
avoidWhen: Internal tools behind single sign-on, where the identity provider enforces these controls
Machine-to-machine APIs, which should use keys or workload identity, not passwords

rows: One attempt per account across millions
Fresh or unique leaks it has not seen
Logins with a correct stolen password
Phishing of OTP codes, unless the factor resists phishing

numbers.title: Why per-IP and per-account limits miss a stuffing run
assumptions: Each attempt targets a different account
Per-IP limit 20 per minute; per-account lockout after 5 failures
steps: Per address: 400,000 / 30,000 ≈ 13 attempts an hour, about 0.2 a minute, far under 20 a minute
Per account: one attempt each, so the 5-failure rule never fires
Takeovers: 400,000 × 0.005 = 2,000 accounts an hour
Site-wide signal: failures far above the normal hourly baseline, which is the alert that fires
numbers.result: Neither limit triggers, yet 2,000 accounts an hour fall. Site-wide anomaly detection, breached-password resets and MFA are what change the outcome.

india.title: What OWASP and NIST recommend
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Credential Stuffing Prevention Cheat Sheet calls multi-factor authentication by far the best defence against password attacks such as credential stuffing and password spraying. It cites a Microsoft analysis suggesting MFA would have stopped 99.9% of account compromises. NIST SP 800-63B-4 requires verifiers to compare new passwords with lists of commonly used or compromised values. It limits consecutive failed attempts on an account to no more than 100. It says verifiers shall not impose composition rules or force periodic changes, and it sets a 15-character minimum for passwords used alone.

pitfalls.trap: Relying on per-IP rate limits for login
pitfalls.say: I would rate-limit on several keys and watch the site-wide failure ratio, because stuffing spreads across addresses.

pitfalls.trap: Locking accounts on a timer after a few failures
pitfalls.say: Throttle and step up instead, so attackers cannot lock real users out.

pitfalls.trap: Different errors for unknown user and wrong password
pitfalls.say: Return one response and equalise timing, including on sign-up and reset.

takeaways: Credential stuffing spreads leaked pairs across addresses and accounts
Throttle and challenge instead of hard lockouts
Uniform responses and timing stop account enumeration
MFA and breached-password checks change the outcome most

interactive.title: Which control stops this run?
interactive.prompt: Tonight’s attack sends 400,000 attempts an hour from 30,000 residential addresses, one attempt per account, using pairs from another site’s breach.

choices.label: A per-IP limit of 20 attempts a minute
choices.feedback: Each address sends about 13 an hour, well under the limit.

choices.label: Locking accounts after 5 failures
choices.feedback: Each account sees one attempt, so the lock never triggers.

choices.label: MFA plus resets for breached passwords
choices.feedback: Right: a correct password is no longer enough, and exposed passwords are retired.

interactive.reveal: Defend against distributed stuffing by devaluing the password, and alert on site-wide failure spikes.

seeAlso.why: Rate limiting algorithms behind the per-key login limits
MFA and passkeys, the control that makes stolen passwords insufficient
Slow password hashing, which creates the timing gap that leaks usernames

title: Designing API Keys: Format, Storage, Scopes and Rotation
objectives: Generate API keys with enough randomness and a recognisable format
Store and verify keys so a database leak exposes nothing usable
Scope, rotate and revoke keys without breaking integrations

cards.title: An API key is a password for a program
cards.body: Whoever presents the key acts as its owner, so treat it as a bearer secret. Send it only over TLS and in a header such as Authorization, never in the URL. URLs end up in server and proxy logs, browser history, analytics and Referer headers, and RFC 6750 says bearer tokens should not go in the query string. An API key identifies a program, not a person. When a user delegates access to a third party, use OAuth instead, so the user can see and revoke it.

cards.title: Random, prefixed, shown once
cards.body: Build the secret from at least 128 bits, and preferably 256 bits (32 bytes), from a cryptographically secure random generator, then encode it. Add a readable prefix such as acme_live_ or acme_test_. People can tell environments apart, and secret scanners can match the pattern with few false positives. A short checksum lets a scanner reject random lookalikes without calling you. Show the full key once at creation; after that show only the prefix and last four characters.

cards.title: Worked example: storing and checking keys
cards.body: A key looks like acme_live_ + key id + secret. The key id is not secret; the secret part is 32 random bytes.
steps: Store the key id, a SHA-256 hash of the secret (or an HMAC with a server-side pepper), the scopes, owner, expiry, and created and last-used times
On a request, parse out the key id and load that one record; no table scan, no secret in the lookup
Hash the presented secret and compare it with the stored hash in constant time
Check revocation, expiry and that the scopes cover this endpoint and method
Update last-used in the background, which later shows which keys are stale or unexpectedly busy

cards.title: Misconception: API keys need a slow password hash
cards.body: Slow hashes such as Argon2id exist because human passwords have little entropy and can be guessed offline. A 256-bit random secret cannot be guessed, even with a fast hash: 2^256 candidates is far beyond any computer. A fast hash keeps verification to microseconds per request. A 100 ms hash at 2,000 requests a second would need about 200 CPU cores just to check keys. The right defence for keys is entropy, not slowness.

cards.title: Trap: one all-powerful key per account
cards.body: One key that can do everything, never expires and is pasted into five integrations means any leak is total. Revoking it also breaks all five at once, so nobody does. Issue a separate, named key for each integration, scoped to the resources and actions it needs, with an optional expiry. Allow two active keys per integration so rotation can overlap. Rate-limit and monitor per key, so one leaked key stands out.

questions.prompt: How should a server store the API keys it issues?

choices.label: A fast hash of the random secret, with its id and scopes
Encrypted, with the key held in the same database
A bcrypt hash at cost 14, checked on each request
In plain text, so support can read keys back to customers

questions.explanation: High-entropy secrets cannot be guessed, so a fast hash is safe and cheap. Encrypting with a key stored beside the data protects little. A cost-14 bcrypt adds roughly a second of CPU to every request for no gain. Plain text turns any database leak into working keys.

questions.prompt: Why send an API key in a request header rather than the URL query string?

choices.label: Headers are encrypted by TLS but URLs are not
URLs end up in logs, history and Referer headers
Query strings cannot hold more than 64 characters
Servers cannot read query strings on POST requests

questions.explanation: Inside TLS, the path, query and headers are all encrypted. The risk is where URLs are recorded after decryption: access logs, proxies, analytics and Referer. Query strings can be long, and servers read them on any method.

questions.prompt: A key’s secret part is 22 characters, each drawn at random from a 64-character alphabet. How many bits of randomness does it carry?
assumptions: 64 possible symbols each, chosen uniformly at random
questions.workedAnswer: log2(64) = 6 bits per character, so 22 × 6 = 132 bits.
questions.explanation: Sanity check: that is above the 128-bit floor. The length alone is not the measure: 22 characters typed by a person would carry far less.

questions.prompt: A partner integration only needs to read order status. What key should it get?

choices.label: The account’s main key, so nothing breaks when scopes change
A copy of an admin’s key, with a note to use it carefully
A separate key named for the partner, scoped to read orders
A read-only database login instead of an API key

questions.explanation: Least privilege limits the damage if the partner leaks the key, and a named key can be revoked without touching anyone else. The main or admin key turns a partner leak into a full compromise. A database login bypasses the API’s own authorisation and exposes far more than order status.

questions.prompt: Order a key rotation that does not break the integration.

items.label: Deploy the new key to the integration
Revoke the old key
Create a second key with the same scopes
Watch last-used times until the old key goes quiet

questions.explanation: Overlap two valid keys, switch, confirm with usage data, and only then revoke.

questions.prompt: A key starting with acme_live_ appears in a public code repository. What makes the prefix useful here?

choices.label: Scanners can recognise the format and alert quickly
The prefix encrypts the rest of the key
Prefixed keys only work from approved addresses
The prefix lets the server skip the hash check

questions.explanation: A distinctive prefix plus checksum lets secret scanners spot leaks with few false positives, so you can revoke within minutes. The prefix is plain text and grants nothing by itself. Address limits are a separate control, and the hash check always runs.

flashcards.back: At least 128 bits from a secure random generator; 256 bits is common.

flashcards.front: Why a fast hash is fine for keys
flashcards.back: Random secrets cannot be guessed, so slowness adds cost without security.
Create a second key, deploy it, watch the old key go quiet, revoke it.

sources.title: OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet
OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023)
RFC 6750: Bearer Token Usage

mechanism.title: The life of an API key
steps: Generate: 32 bytes from a CSPRNG, encoded without ambiguity, plus a non-secret key id. Add a prefix naming the product and environment, and a short checksum.
Display once: show the full key at creation and store only its hash. If the customer loses it, they create a new one; you cannot and should not recover it.
Transmit: always over TLS, in the Authorization header. Reject keys sent in query strings instead of quietly accepting them, so the habit never forms.
Verify: look up by key id, hash the secret, compare in constant time, then check revocation, expiry, scopes and any address or referrer limits.
Limit and observe: apply rate limits and quotas per key, log the key id (never the secret) with each request, and alert on sudden changes in volume or source networks.

Rotate and respond: allow two active keys, show last-used times, and give customers a one-click revoke. Watch public repositories for your prefix and revoke leaked keys on the spot, then tell the owner.

useWhen: Server-to-server integrations owned by one customer account
Usage metering and per-client rate limits on a public API
avoidWhen: A user granting a third-party app access to their data (use OAuth)
Code running in a browser or mobile app, where any key is public by design

rows: Bearer secret: leaks are usable until revoked
More moving parts; short lifetimes need refresh
Proving integrity and freshness of each call

numbers.title: Why entropy beats slow hashing for keys
assumptions: Secret part: 22 characters from a 64-symbol alphabet
Attacker with a stolen hash table can test 10^12 candidates a second (very generous)
steps: Entropy: 22 × 6 = 132 bits, so 2^132 ≈ 5.4 × 10^39 candidates
Search time: 5.4 × 10^39 / 10^12 ≈ 5.4 × 10^27 seconds ≈ 1.7 × 10^20 years for the whole space
Slow hash cost: at 100 ms each, 2,000 × 0.1 = 200 CPU-seconds every second, so about 200 cores
Fast hash cost: at about 1 µs each, 2,000 × 10^-6 = 0.002 cores
numbers.result: Random keys are safe with a fast hash, and a slow hash would burn about 200 cores for no extra security.

india.title: OWASP guidance on API keys
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet recommends requiring API keys on protected endpoints and returning 429 Too Many Requests when a key exceeds its rate. It also recommends revoking keys that break the usage agreement, and not relying on API keys alone to protect sensitive, critical or high-value resources. The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) lists broken authentication as API2. RFC 6750 says bearer tokens should not be passed in page URLs, because URLs are often logged.

pitfalls.trap: Storing API keys in plain text so support can look them up
pitfalls.say: I would store only a hash and show the key once; a lost key is replaced, not recovered.

pitfalls.trap: Using a slow password hash for every API request
pitfalls.say: The key’s 128+ bits of randomness is the defence; a fast hash keeps verification cheap.

pitfalls.trap: Shipping an API key inside a mobile app
pitfalls.say: Anything in the app can be extracted, so use per-user tokens issued after login instead.

takeaways: Keys are bearer secrets: TLS, headers, never URLs
At least 128 random bits with a recognisable prefix
Store a hash with the id and scopes; show the key once
Scope keys per integration and rotate with two active keys

interactive.title: What does the table leak expose?
interactive.prompt: An attacker copies the api_keys table. Each row holds a key id, the SHA-256 of a 256-bit random secret, scopes and owner.

choices.label: No working keys: the hashes cannot be turned back into secrets
choices.feedback: Right: with 256 random bits, guessing is hopeless even with a fast hash.

choices.label: Every key, because SHA-256 is fast to compute
choices.feedback: Speed matters only when the input is guessable; these secrets are not.

choices.label: The keys of accounts with short usernames
choices.feedback: Usernames play no part in the secret.

interactive.reveal: The metadata still leaks (who has which scopes), so review it, but no request can be authenticated with what was taken.

seeAlso.why: Where services keep the API keys they use to call others
Password hashing, and why low-entropy secrets need slow hashes
Per-key rate limits and quotas on a public API

title: Security Logging for Detection and Tamper Evidence
objectives: Choose the security events that reveal an attacker’s path
Keep security logs that survive an intruder with admin access
Keep secrets out of logs and turn logs into alerts with owners

cards.title: Log the steps an attacker has to take
cards.body: Security logging is for spotting and reconstructing an attack. Attackers have to sign in, often after many failures, then try things they are not allowed to do, raise their privileges, weaken defences and take data. So log failed and successful logins, authorisation denials, MFA and password changes, role grants, new keys and tokens, security configuration changes and large exports. Give each event an actor id, action, target, outcome, UTC time and source, so events can be joined into a story. Product audit trails for customers and support staff are a related topic, covered in the Backend lessons.

cards.title: An audit trail must survive the attacker
cards.body: An intruder with admin rights on a server can edit or delete local logs. Ship security events off the host within seconds to a store in a separate account. Make that store append-only or write-once for a retention period, with delete rights held by nobody in day-to-day operations. Then add tamper evidence, such as a hash chain with signed checkpoints, so any edit that slips through can be detected.

cards.title: Worked example: hash-chaining audit records
cards.body: A payments platform needs to prove that its admin-action log has not been edited.
steps: Each record stores the hash of the record before it
Record n’s hash = SHA-256(record n’s contents + record n−1’s hash)
Every hour, sign the latest hash and store the signed checkpoint in a separate system
To verify, recompute the chain from the last trusted checkpoint and compare
An edited or deleted record breaks every hash after it, and the checkpoint will not match

cards.title: Misconception: log everything, just in case
cards.body: Logging full requests and responses captures passwords, session cookies, bearer tokens, card numbers and personal data. The log store then becomes a richer target than the database, and is usually less protected. Log identifiers and outcomes instead: user 8812 exported invoice 5531, success. Redact known secret fields in the logging library, so a careless call cannot leak them. Mask or tokenise personal data you do need.

cards.title: Edge case: changes that skip the application
cards.body: Audit records written by application code miss changes made straight in the database, such as a migration, a support script or an attacker with a database login. A trigger on the sensitive tables can insert an audit row in the same transaction as each change, so the change and its audit row commit or roll back together. Record the database role, and the acting user when the application sets one, for example with SET LOCAL app.actor_id in PostgreSQL. A table owner can still disable the trigger or edit the audit table, so the application role should only be able to insert into it, and its rows should be shipped off the database like other security events.

cards.title: Trap: logs nobody reads
cards.body: Collected but unwatched logs only help after someone else tells you about the breach. Write detections for high-signal events, such as an admin role granted outside change windows, MFA removed and then a login from a new network, a key used from a new country, or bursts of 403s on sequential object ids. Give each alert an owner and a runbook. Keep logs longer than it takes you to discover incidents, or the evidence expires first.

questions.prompt: Which event belongs in a security audit log?

choices.label: A cache miss on the product catalogue
An admin grants a user the billing-admin role
A slow-query warning on a reporting replica
A health check returning 200 to the load balancer

questions.explanation: Privilege changes are a classic investigation question: who gave this account its power, and when? Cache, performance and health signals belong in operational telemetry, not the audit trail.

questions.prompt: An attacker with root on the app server wants to hide their actions. Which setup best preserves the evidence?

choices.label: Logs written to a local file only the root account may modify
Logs rotated daily, compressed and kept on the same disk for a year
Logs shipped within seconds to a write-once store in another account
Logs encrypted on the server with a key from its own config

questions.explanation: Evidence must leave the attacker’s reach before they can touch it. Root can edit root-only files, rotated logs on the same disk, and anything encrypted with a key on that server.

questions.prompt: A hash-chained audit log lives on a server the attacker controls. Why also sign the latest hash hourly and store it elsewhere?

choices.label: The attacker can rewrite the chain but not forge the checkpoint
Signing makes the log entries unreadable to the attacker
Hash chains cannot be verified without a signature
Signed checkpoints compress the chain so that it takes up less disk

questions.explanation: Someone who controls the log can recompute every hash after an edit, so a chain alone proves little. An external, signed checkpoint pins the chain to a value the attacker cannot change. Signing does not hide content or save space, and chains are verifiable by recomputation.

questions.prompt: A debug flag logs full request headers in production. What is the most serious result?

choices.label: Log storage costs rise by a few percent each month
Response times double across the service
Timestamps in the log drift out of order
Live session tokens become readable to log users

questions.explanation: Anyone who can read logs can now replay live sessions. That reaches far more people than can read the database. Cost and latency effects are minor, and logging headers does not reorder timestamps.

questions.prompt: A service handles 2,000 requests a second. 5% of them are security events (logins, writes, admin actions), each logged as a 500-byte record. How many GB of audit records is that per day?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: logging every request instead would be 20 times more (86.4 GB). Audit-only records are small enough to keep for a year.

questions.prompt: An alert fires: a user’s MFA was removed and a new API key created from an unfamiliar network. Order the response.

items.label: Scope: review everything the key and sessions touched
Confirm the alert against the audit trail
Recover: restore MFA, reset credentials and record the timeline
Contain: revoke the new key and the user’s sessions

questions.explanation: Confirm quickly, contain before investigating at length, then scope the damage and recover. The audit trail drives each step.

flashcards.back: Login failures, authorisation denials, MFA and role changes, new keys, config changes, large exports.

flashcards.front: How do you protect logs from an intruder?
flashcards.back: Ship off-host fast to a write-once store in another account; add hash chains with signed checkpoints.
Passwords, tokens, session ids, keys, card numbers and unmasked personal data.

sources.title: OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet
OWASP Logging Vocabulary Cheat Sheet
NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

mechanism.title: From event to evidence to alert
steps: Define the events: authentication, authorisation failures, privilege changes, sensitive reads and exports, admin actions, key and secret lifecycle, and configuration changes. Use a shared vocabulary such as OWASP’s, so “authn_login_fail” means the same in every service.
Structure each record: actor id, action, target, outcome, UTC timestamp, source address, service and request or trace id. Structured fields can be queried; free text cannot.

Redact at the source: the logging library drops or masks fields named password, token, authorisation, cookie and secret, and personal data is tokenised. Fixing it downstream is too late, because copies already exist.
Ship and protect: stream to a separate account within seconds, write-once for the retention period, with tight read access. Hash-chain batches and sign checkpoints into another system.

Detect: rules and baselines over the stream, such as privilege grants, MFA removals, impossible travel, export spikes and runs of authorisation failures. Each alert has an owner, a severity and a runbook.

Retain and review: keep security events at least as long as your realistic time to detect, often a year or more. Test the trail by replaying a mock incident and checking that every question can be answered.

useWhen: Any system with user accounts, money or personal data
Regulated environments that must prove who did what
avoidWhen: High-volume debug output, which belongs in short-lived operational logs
Raw request bodies on endpoints that carry secrets or personal data

rows: Field lists to maintain as code changes
Incidents found in hours, not months
Tuning to keep false alarms low

numbers.title: How big is a year of audit logs?
assumptions: Compression of about 10× on structured text (illustrative)
steps: Events: 2,000 × 0.05 = 100 per second
Daily volume: 100 events/s at 500 bytes is 50,000 bytes/s, and 50,000 × 86,400 = 4,320,000,000 bytes, about 4.3 GB a day
Yearly: 4.32 × 365 ≈ 1,577 GB ≈ 1.6 TB raw
Compressed: about 160 GB a year at 10×
numbers.result: A year of audit-only events fits in roughly 160 GB, so short retention is rarely a storage problem; it is a choice.

india.title: OWASP on what to log and what not to
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet lists events to always record. They include input validation failures, authentication successes and failures, authorisation failures, session management failures, application errors, and use of higher-risk functions such as user administration and data import or export. It also lists data that should usually not be recorded directly. That includes session identifiers, access tokens, passwords, encryption keys, database connection strings and sensitive personal data. The OWASP Top 10:2025 keeps logging as a category, now named Security Logging and Alerting Failures.

pitfalls.trap: Logging whole request bodies for debugging in production
pitfalls.say: I would log ids and outcomes and redact secret fields in the logging library itself.

pitfalls.trap: Keeping audit logs on the same host as the application
pitfalls.say: Stream them off-host to a write-once store, because an intruder with root can edit anything local.

pitfalls.trap: Seven days of retention to save money
pitfalls.say: Retention must cover the time it takes to detect incidents, and audit events are small.

takeaways: Log the events an attacker’s path must produce, with actor, target and outcome
Move logs off-host to write-once storage, with tamper evidence
Redact secrets and personal data at the source
Detections with owners turn logs into early warnings

interactive.title: Can you tell what happened?
interactive.prompt: On day 20 you learn customer data was exported. Your logs hold only access lines (method, path, status) with no user ids, and retention is 7 days.

choices.label: No: the records have expired, and they never named the actor
choices.feedback: Right: both retention and missing fields defeat the investigation.

choices.label: Yes: the access lines show the export path
choices.feedback: They expired on day 7, and they never said who called it.

choices.label: Yes, if the load balancer kept its own logs
choices.feedback: Those lack user ids too, and usually have similar retention.

interactive.reveal: Log the actor and target for security events, and keep them longer than your realistic time to detect.

seeAlso.why: General logging and metrics, the operational side of the same pipeline
Authorisation failures are among the most useful events to log
Security incident response uses these logs to scope a compromise
Product audit trails in code: actor context, impersonation and customer activity logs
History tables and the triggers that record row changes inside the database

title: Tenant Isolation: Preventing Cross-Tenant Data Leaks
objectives: Find the paths where one tenant’s request can reach another tenant’s data
Carry a verified tenant context through services, jobs, caches and files
Prove isolation with cross-tenant tests, canary tenants and per-tenant keys

cards.title: Where cross-tenant leaks actually come from
cards.body: Whichever data layout you choose, shared tables or a database per tenant, the leaks come from the same places: a lookup by id with no tenant scope, a tenant id taken from client input, a background job that loses or reuses the tenant context, a cache key, search index or file path without the tenant in it, and support or export tools with access to everyone. One such bug exposes many customers at once, and their customers too, which is why a cross-tenant leak is usually the most serious incident a SaaS product can have.

cards.title: Tenant context comes from the credential, not the request
cards.body: The tenant a request acts for must come from something the server verified, such as the session or a signed token’s tenant claim. It must never come from a header, query parameter or body field the client can change. A subdomain such as acme.example.com is fine for routing, but the server must still check that the authenticated user belongs to that tenant. Carry the verified tenant through internal calls and background jobs, not just the first hop.

cards.title: Worked example: keeping one tenant’s export inside its boundary
cards.body: A user asks for a CSV export of their workspace. The work happens in a background job, and the file is downloaded later.
steps: The API verifies the token, checks the user belongs to tenant Acme, and queues a job carrying Acme’s id from the verified session
The worker sets the tenant context from the job before its first query, and clears it when the job ends
Queries run through the tenant-scoped data layer, so every read is filtered to Acme
The file is written under exports/acme/…, never a shared folder with a guessable name
The download link is short-lived, and the server checks the requester still belongs to Acme before serving it

cards.title: Misconception: separate databases make cross-tenant leaks impossible
cards.body: Silos protect the main tables, but data also lives elsewhere. A connection cache can route a request to the wrong tenant’s database. Shared caches, search indexes, queues, object-storage paths and analytics exports may not carry a tenant key at all. Each of these needs the tenant in its key or path, and a test. Isolation is a property of the whole data path, not of the primary database.

cards.title: Trap: no test ever plays the other tenant
cards.body: Most test suites sign in as one user and check that features work. Isolation needs the opposite: two fixture tenants, and for every endpoint, export and report a test where tenant A asks for tenant B’s ids and expects not found. In production, seed a canary tenant with distinctive marker records and alert if a marker ever appears in another tenant’s responses, exports or logs. Log every cross-tenant denial with both the caller’s tenant and the target, so probing stands out.

questions.prompt: Where should a request’s tenant id come from?

choices.label: An X-Tenant-Id header the client sends
The verified session or token of the caller
The subdomain alone, such as acme.example.com
A tenant field in the JSON request body

questions.explanation: Only server-verified credentials are trustworthy. Headers and body fields are attacker-controlled. A subdomain is useful for routing but must be checked against the caller’s membership, or a user of one tenant can simply change the hostname.

questions.prompt: Dashboard responses are cached under the key /api/dashboard?range=7d. Customers start seeing other companies’ figures. What is the fix?

choices.label: Shorten the cache lifetime from an hour to a minute
Put the verified tenant id in the cache key
Add row-level security to the dashboard tables
Encrypt the cached responses at rest

questions.explanation: The key identifies the query but not whose data it holds, so the first tenant’s answer is served to everyone. A shorter lifetime only shrinks the window. Database policies never run on a cache hit. Encryption at rest protects stolen disks, not responses served to the wrong tenant.

questions.prompt: Each tenant’s records are encrypted with that tenant’s own data key, chosen by the row’s tenant id. A bug copies a row of tenant A into tenant B’s data. What happens when B reads it?

choices.label: B reads it normally, since the same server holds both keys
The read uses A’s key automatically and succeeds
Decryption with B’s key fails, and the error can raise an alert
The database refuses to store a row encrypted with another key

questions.explanation: The row now carries B’s tenant id, so the app picks B’s key, and authenticated decryption fails instead of showing A’s data. Holding both keys does not matter, because the key is chosen by tenant. Nothing selects A’s key for a row labelled B. The database stores ciphertext without knowing which key made it.

questions.prompt: A nightly job emails each tenant a usage summary. It sets the tenant context once, before looping over all tenants. What goes wrong?

choices.label: Every email shows the first tenant’s figures
The job fails because the context is set too early
Each email shows the figures for all tenants combined
Nothing, since the loop passes each tenant id along

questions.explanation: Every query in the loop runs under the first tenant’s context, so each customer receives that tenant’s data. Setting it early raises no error. Combined figures would need a query with no tenant filter at all. Passing ids in the loop does not help when queries read the context, which never changes. Set and clear the context for each tenant inside the loop.

questions.prompt: You have 120 endpoints and 3 roles. Each cross-tenant test checks one endpoint for one role in one direction, A against B or B against A. How many tests is that?
assumptions: 2 directions: A against B, and B against A
questions.explanation: Design implication: at about 50 ms each, 720 tests take about 36 seconds, cheap enough to run on every pull request. Generate them from the route list so a new endpoint cannot skip them.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that keep a background export inside one tenant.

items.label: Set the tenant context in the worker before the first query
Check membership again before serving the download
Verify the token and check the user belongs to the tenant
Write the file under a path that starts with the tenant
Queue the job with the tenant id taken from the verified session

questions.explanation: The tenant is verified once, then travels with the job, scopes every query and file, and is checked again when someone collects the result.

flashcards.front: Where does the tenant id come from?
flashcards.back: The verified session or token, never a client-supplied field.
A tenant seeded with marker records; an alert fires if a marker shows up anywhere else.
A row copied into the wrong tenant fails to decrypt, and one tenant’s data can be crypto-shredded on exit.

mechanism.title: Isolation along the whole request path
steps: Identity: authenticate the user, then resolve their tenant memberships on the server. The active tenant is one the user belongs to, chosen from the token or session.

Propagation: pass the verified tenant in a signed internal token or request context to every downstream service, queue message and scheduled job. Jobs that process many tenants set and clear the context for each one inside the loop.

Data enforcement: route every read and write through one tenant-scoped data layer, with a database backstop such as row-level security where the design allows. The data models themselves are covered in the Databases and System Design lessons.

Side channels: put the tenant in every cache key, search index filter, object path, queue topic and download link, and treat support and export tools as cross-tenant by design, with their own approvals and logs.

Per-tenant keys: encrypt each tenant’s data with its own key, chosen by tenant and bound to the tenant id as associated data, so misplaced rows fail to decrypt and a departing tenant can be crypto-shredded.

Verification: generate cross-tenant tests for every endpoint and export, seed canary tenants with marker records, and log denials with both the caller tenant and the target tenant so probing stands out.

useWhen: Any SaaS where customers’ data must never mix
Enterprise customers who ask how isolation is proved, not just promised
avoidWhen: Single-tenant deployments, where the boundary is the deployment itself
Treating per-tenant keys as a substitute for authorisation checks

rows: Caches, files and tools that bypass it
Tenant in every key and path
Code that builds keys by hand
Per-tenant keys bound to the tenant id
Rows copied to the wrong tenant
Bugs that decrypt under the right tenant and then leak
Paths no test or canary exercises

numbers.title: How cheap is proving isolation?
assumptions: Tests in both directions between two fixture tenants
steps: Tests: 120 × 3 = 360 endpoint-role checks; 360 × 2 = 720 counting both directions
Time: 720 × 50 ms = 36,000 ms, which is 36 seconds
Compare: one cross-tenant leak in a pool of 5,000 tenants can expose every one of them
So the tests run on every pull request, and the canary watches production
numbers.result: In this illustrative setup, full cross-tenant coverage costs about 36 seconds of CI time per change.

india.title: AWS and OWASP guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The AWS SaaS Tenant Isolation Strategies whitepaper treats isolation as something enforced at every layer, not only in the database, and stresses that tenant context should come from the authenticated identity rather than from values a caller can change. The OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet asks for permission checks on every request and denial by default, and the OWASP Authorization Testing Automation Cheat Sheet describes generating access tests from a matrix of endpoints and roles, which is the same idea as the cross-tenant matrix above.

pitfalls.trap: Taking the tenant id from a request header
pitfalls.say: I derive it from the verified token and check membership; client-supplied tenant ids are just input.

pitfalls.trap: Setting tenant context once for a job that loops over tenants
pitfalls.say: Set and clear it for each tenant inside the loop.

pitfalls.trap: Forgetting the cache, search index and export files
pitfalls.say: Put the tenant in every key and path, and include them in cross-tenant tests.

takeaways: Leaks come from unscoped lookups, lost context and side channels
The tenant comes from verified credentials and travels with every call
Per-tenant keys make misplaced data fail closed
Prove isolation with cross-tenant tests and canary tenants

interactive.title: What does the user see?
interactive.prompt: Search suggestions are built from one shared index of document titles across all tenants. Results pages filter by tenant, but the suggestion list does not. A user types “acq”.

choices.label: Titles from other tenants, such as a rival’s acquisition plan
choices.feedback: Right: the unfiltered suggestion list leaks other tenants’ titles.

choices.label: Only their own titles, because results are filtered
choices.feedback: Only the results page filters; suggestions come straight from the shared index.

choices.label: No suggestions, because the index is shared
choices.feedback: A shared index returns everyone’s matches unless something filters them.

interactive.reveal: Apply the tenant filter in every read path, suggestions, counts and facets included, and add them to the cross-tenant tests.

seeAlso.why: Object-level access checks, the per-request half of tenant isolation
Envelope encryption, the basis for per-tenant keys
Tenant boundaries are the outermost authorisation rule
Noisy neighbours: the performance side of sharing infrastructure between tenants
Tenant ids in the schema and row-level security policies that enforce them in the database

title: Defending Against Bots and Automated Abuse
objectives: Name the automated threat a business flow faces
Combine signals into a risk score instead of trusting one check
Raise the attacker’s cost without punishing real users

cards.title: Name the abuse, not just the bot
cards.body: The OWASP Automated Threats project names more than twenty abuses of legitimate features. Carding tests stolen cards with small payments. Scalping buys limited stock for resale. Scraping copies content or prices. Account creation farms fake sign-ups for referral rewards or spam. Denial of inventory holds stock in carts without paying. Each one uses requests that look valid, so the defence depends on the flow being abused. Some bots are welcome, such as verified search crawlers, uptime monitors and partner integrations, so identify those and let them through.

cards.title: Signals, scored together
cards.body: No single signal is reliable. Combine many: attempt rates per account, device, card and network; whether the address belongs to a data centre or a residential proxy pool; whether headers and TLS fingerprint match the browser claimed; behaviour such as impossible typing speed; and outcome ratios, like the share of payments declined. Feed them into a risk score per request or session, and act on the score, not on any one rule.

cards.title: Worked example: stopping card testing at checkout
cards.body: Guest checkout suddenly sees thousands of tiny payments, most of them declined.
steps: Alert on the spike in the decline ratio, not on request volume alone
Cap attempts per card, device, account and network over an hour and a day
Step up risky payments to cardholder verification or an extra challenge
Delay fulfilment of small first-time orders from risky sessions
Feed confirmed fraud and chargebacks back into the risk score

cards.title: Misconception: a CAPTCHA stops bots
cards.body: Solving services clear challenges for a small fee per thousand, and solver models handle many puzzles directly. Meanwhile, CAPTCHAs slow real customers and exclude people who rely on assistive technology. Treat a challenge as one rung on a ladder, shown only when the risk score is high, and make the abuse unprofitable in other ways, such as delaying referral rewards until an account shows real activity.

cards.title: Trap: blocking loudly
cards.body: A clear “403 bot detected” tells the operator exactly which check fired, and they adapt within hours. Prefer quieter responses where you can: slow the session, show a challenge, accept the sign-up but withhold its reward, or return plausible but useless results. Measure success by business outcomes, such as fake accounts, declined payments or scraped volume, not by the number of requests blocked.

questions.prompt: Resellers’ scripts fill carts with concert tickets and hold them until the timer runs out, so fans see them as sold out. Which automated threat is this?

choices.label: Scraping
Denial of inventory
Credential stuffing
Carding

questions.explanation: Holding stock without buying it denies it to others. Scraping copies data, credential stuffing replays leaked passwords, and carding tests stolen cards. Scalping, buying the stock to resell, is the related threat that often follows.

questions.prompt: Guest checkout sees 40,000 payment attempts in an hour, 95% declined, mostly for tiny amounts. What is the best first response?

choices.label: Block the country that sent the most attempts
Turn off guest checkout for all customers for a month
Cap attempts per card and device; challenge risky payments
Raise the minimum order value to discourage small orders

questions.explanation: This is card testing, and limits on the card and device attack its economics while real customers barely notice. Attackers rotate proxies, so a country block mostly hurts real buyers there. Removing guest checkout loses sales for a month. A minimum order value changes little, since testers can pay more.

questions.prompt: Why does a CAPTCHA on the sign-up form, on its own, fail against a determined fake-account farm?

choices.label: Solver services and models clear challenges cheaply
Farms send requests too slowly to ever trigger a challenge
Sign-up forms are rarely a target for automation
CAPTCHAs are shown only to users on mobile devices

questions.explanation: Challenges are a cost, and for this abuse the cost is tiny. A challenge shown at sign-up applies at any speed. Sign-up is a top target, for referral rewards and spam. CAPTCHAs are shown on any device the site chooses.

questions.prompt: Illustrative prices: an operator pays $2 per 1,000 CAPTCHA solves and earns $0.50 per fake account, which needs 3 solves. How much do the solves cost them per 1,000 accounts?
questions.formula: accounts × solves per account × price per solve
questions.explanation: Design implication: friction costing about 1% of the payoff deters nobody. Cut the payoff instead, for example by paying referral rewards only after real purchases.

questions.prompt: Order these responses from least to most friction for a real user who is wrongly flagged.

items.label: Run an invisible check such as a browser proof-of-work
Observe and score the session silently
Block, or require a verified identity
Slow it down with rate limits or small delays
Show an interactive challenge

questions.explanation: Climb the ladder only as far as the risk score demands, so most false positives feel no friction at all and real attackers face rising cost.

questions.prompt: A price-comparison company scrapes your whole catalogue each night, adding 30% to traffic and leaking promotions early.
constraints: Shoppers must not notice any change
Some partners want the data legitimately

approaches.label: Per-client rate limits, headless-browser detection and a paid data feed
Block all data centre address ranges
Put the catalogue behind a login

rationaleOptions.label: A paid feed turns the cost into revenue and removes the incentive
Per-client limits cap cost without touching normal shoppers
Data centre blocks stop scrapers that use residential proxies
A login wall costs nothing in lost customers

rationaleConflicts.r3: Residential proxies are exactly how scrapers avoid data centre blocks.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Shoppers browse before signing in, and search engines cannot index a login wall.

questions.explanation: Raise the cost of the abusive path and offer a legitimate path to anyone who will pay for the data.

flashcards.back: Testing stolen cards with small payments; watch decline ratios.
Each is easy to fake; combine them into a risk score.
Observe, slow, invisible check, challenge, block: climb only as risk demands.

sources.title: OWASP Automated Threats to Web Applications
OWASP API6:2023 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
OWASP Credential Stuffing Prevention Cheat Sheet

mechanism.title: How an abuse defence works
steps: Map the flows worth abusing: sign-up, login, checkout, gift cards, search, price pages, limited stock and referral rewards. For each flow, write down which automated threat applies and what a successful attack earns, because the payoff decides how hard attackers will push.

Instrument outcomes: record for each flow the business result as well as the request, such as accounts that never act, payments declined, carts abandoned at the timer or pages fetched per session. Abuse shows up in outcomes long before it shows up in request rates.

Score risk: combine rate counters per account, device, card and network with reputation, fingerprint consistency and behaviour into a score per session. Retrain or retune it with confirmed abuse and with complaints from real users who were wrongly flagged.
Respond on a ladder: let low scores through untouched, slow or invisibly check medium scores, and challenge or block only high scores. Prefer quiet responses that do not reveal which signal fired.
