Change the economics: delay rewards until real activity, hold risky orders, limit purchases per buyer for scarce stock, and offer paid or partner access for data that people will otherwise scrape.

Review and adapt: attackers change tools within days, so watch the outcome metrics after each change, keep an allowlist of verified good bots, and treat the defence as an ongoing operation rather than a project.

useWhen: Flows with a direct payoff: payments, rewards, scarce stock, valuable data
Sites where fake accounts or scraping already show up in business metrics
avoidWhen: Adding challenges for all users when abuse is limited to one flow
Relying on a single vendor score without checking business outcomes

rows: Capping attempts per card, device or account
Flagging data centres and spoofed clients
Adding time or a fee per attempt
Needs product changes, not just security

numbers.title: What does card testing cost a merchant?
assumptions: A processor fee of $0.10 per attempt, illustrative
Caps per card and device stop 90% of attempts
steps: Overnight: 4,000 × 8 = $32,000 in fees alone
With caps, 10% get through: 32,000 × 0.1 = $3,200
Processors may also raise fees or end the account if decline rates stay high
numbers.result: Simple caps cut the illustrative overnight fee bill from about $32,000 to about $3,200, before counting chargebacks.

india.title: OWASP Automated Threats to Web Applications
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Automated Threats to Web Applications project publishes a handbook that names automated threat events, such as OAT-001 Carding, OAT-005 Scalping, OAT-008 Credential Stuffing, OAT-010 Card Cracking and OAT-012 Cashing Out. Its examples show organisations writing requirements in terms of these threat events, for instance that payment functions must not be open to carding or card cracking, rather than naming a product. OWASP’s API Security Top 10 makes the same point as API6:2023, Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows.

pitfalls.trap: Measuring success by requests blocked
pitfalls.say: Measure fake accounts, declined payments and scraped volume, because blocked counts rise as attackers retry.

pitfalls.trap: Adding a CAPTCHA and calling it done
pitfalls.say: Use challenges as one rung on a ladder, and remove the payoff that makes abuse worth it.

pitfalls.trap: Returning an explicit bot error
pitfalls.say: Respond quietly, with delays, challenges or withheld rewards, so attackers cannot see which signal fired.

takeaways: Name the threat for each abused flow
Score many signals together
Climb a friction ladder only as risk demands
Make abuse unprofitable, and measure business outcomes

interactive.title: What does the operator do next?
interactive.prompt: You return 403 “bot detected” to any request missing a header that normal browsers send.

choices.label: Adds the header within hours and carries on
choices.feedback: Right: the error told them exactly what to fix.

choices.label: Gives up, since the site clearly detects bots
choices.feedback: Abuse is a business; a cheap fix is worth making.

choices.label: Switches to slower, manual abuse
choices.feedback: Not while an automated fix is this easy.

interactive.reveal: Respond quietly and combine signals, so one change on the attacker’s side does not undo the defence.

seeAlso.why: Credential stuffing is the login form of automated abuse
Rate limiting is the first rung of the friction ladder
APIs expose business flows to the same automation
Network-level floods and amplification, which bot defences at the application layer sit behind

title: Vulnerability Triage and Patch Management
objectives: Separate severity scores from real-world risk
Use exploitation evidence, exposure and reachability to set order
Set patch deadlines a team can actually meet

cards.title: Severity is not the same as risk
cards.body: A CVSS base score (0 to 10) describes how bad a vulnerability would be in a typical setup: how it is reached, what privileges it needs and what it affects. It does not say whether anyone is exploiting it, whether your service is exposed, or whether your code even calls the flawed function. Risk is likelihood times impact in your context, and the score is only one input to it.

cards.title: Signals of likelihood: known exploitation and EPSS
cards.body: Two public signals help with likelihood. CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue lists flaws with evidence of exploitation in the wild. FIRST’s Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) estimates the probability that a flaw will see exploitation activity in the next 30 days. Combine them with exposure: an internet-facing gateway with a known-exploited flaw outranks a higher-scored flaw in an internal batch tool.

cards.title: Worked example: triaging 1,200 scanner findings
cards.body: A container scan across 60 images reports 1,200 findings. The team can fix about 25 a week.
steps: Deduplicate: the same library flaw in 40 images is one fix, which cuts the list to about 300 distinct items
Pull to the top anything that is known-exploited or has a high exploitation probability
Check exposure and reachability: is the component internet-facing, and does untrusted input reach the vulnerable code?
Set a deadline by tier, such as days for exposed and exploited, weeks for exposed, the normal cycle for the rest
Record each accepted risk with an owner, a reason and an expiry date

cards.title: Misconception: “critical” means drop everything
cards.body: Take a 9.8 in a test library that never ships, and a 7.5 that is being exploited in your VPN appliance. The second is the emergency. Treating every high score as urgent burns the team out and buries the few findings that matter. Rank by exploitation evidence, exposure and reachability, and use the score to break ties.

cards.title: Trap: wanting to patch fast without being able to
cards.body: Most delay is not in deciding but in shipping. Typical causes are an unknown inventory, no automated tests to trust an upgrade, and manual deploys. Keep a software bill of materials, so you know where a component runs within minutes of an advisory. Take routine dependency updates in small, tested steps every week, so an urgent bump is ordinary work rather than a leap across two years of versions.

questions.prompt: What does a CVSS base score of 9.8 tell you on its own?

choices.label: The flaw is being actively exploited in the wild right now
Your service calls the vulnerable code
The flaw would be severe if exploited in a typical setup
The vendor’s patch is safe to deploy untested

questions.explanation: The base score describes intrinsic severity. Exploitation evidence comes from sources such as the KEV catalogue, reachability from your own analysis, and patch safety from your tests.

questions.prompt: Finding one: CVSS 9.1 in a library no exposed service loads. Finding two: CVSS 7.2, on the known-exploited list, in your internet-facing gateway. Which first?

choices.label: The 9.1, because the higher base score sets the order
The 7.2 gateway flaw, despite its lower base score
Both together in one release next quarter
Neither until a second scanner confirms them

questions.explanation: Active exploitation plus internet exposure makes the gateway flaw the likely breach. The base score alone ignores both. Waiting a quarter or for a second scanner leaves an exploited, exposed hole open.

questions.prompt: A scanner flags a parsing flaw in a library your build includes. What reduces its urgency most?

choices.label: The library is popular and actively maintained
The service runs inside a container
Evidence that no untrusted input reaches that parser
The finding has been open a while without incident

questions.explanation: If attacker-controlled data cannot reach the flawed code, it cannot be exploited through that path. You still patch, but on the normal cycle. Popularity, containers and quiet history do not stop an exploit that can reach the code.

questions.prompt: You have 300 open findings and fix 25 a week, while 15 new ones arrive each week. How many weeks until the backlog is clear?
questions.formula: backlog / (fixed per week − new per week)
questions.workedAnswer: Net progress is 25 − 15 = 10 a week, so 300 / 10 = 30 weeks.
questions.explanation: Sanity check: ignoring new arrivals gives 12 weeks, a plan that will slip badly. To clear it in 10 weeks you need 300 / 10 + 15 = 45 fixes a week.

questions.prompt: Order a triage pass over a new scanner report.

items.label: Set a fix deadline by tier
Group duplicate findings into single fixes
Check exposure and reachability for each item
Track accepted risks with an owner and expiry
Raise exploited and likely-exploited items to the top

questions.explanation: Shrink the list, rank by likelihood, refine with your own context, then commit to dates and record the exceptions.

questions.prompt: A critical, actively exploited flaw hits the web server software on 400 internet-facing hosts. The vendor fix is out, and your normal release window is monthly.

approaches.label: Mitigate within hours, then roll out the fix within days
Wait for the monthly window to keep change control simple
Put the hosts behind a VPN for good and skip the patch

rationaleOptions.label: Known exploitation makes delay the larger risk
A mitigation buys time while the patch is tested
Change windows matter more than exposure
A network move removes the need to patch

rationaleConflicts.r3: An exploited, exposed flaw is exactly the case emergency change exists for.
rationaleConflicts.r4: The flaw is still there for anyone who reaches the VPN, and public sites cannot hide anyway.

questions.explanation: Exploited and exposed means emergency: mitigate now (a WAF rule or disabling the feature), patch fast, verify.

flashcards.back: CVSS rates severity in general; risk adds exploitation, exposure and reachability in your system.
KEV: evidence of exploitation in the wild. EPSS: probability of exploitation activity in 30 days.
Weeks to clear = backlog / (fix rate − arrival rate).

sources.title: NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4: Enterprise Patch Management Planning
OWASP Vulnerable Dependency Management Cheat Sheet
OWASP Top 10:2025, Software Supply Chain Failures

mechanism.title: A triage pipeline that keeps up
steps: Inventory: generate a software bill of materials for every build and image, and keep a list of what is deployed where. Without it, every advisory starts with a hunt.
Collect: scanners for dependencies, images and hosts feed one queue. Deduplicate by component and version, so one upgrade closes many findings.
Enrich: add the CVSS score, known-exploited status, EPSS probability, and your own context, such as internet exposure, data sensitivity and whether the vulnerable function is reachable.
Decide: map each finding to a tier with a deadline, and choose a response. Patch or upgrade; mitigate (configuration change, WAF rule, disabling a feature); or accept with an owner and an expiry.
Ship: small, frequent dependency updates through automated tests and staged rollout, so urgent fixes use the same path as routine ones.
Measure: track time to remediate by tier and the backlog trend. If arrivals outpace fixes, the plan is fiction, so add capacity or reduce the attack surface.

useWhen: Any team running third-party code, which is every team
Regulated environments that must show patch timelines
avoidWhen: Treating every scanner finding as an emergency, which drowns the real ones
Waivers with no expiry, which quietly become permanent

rows: Whether it is exploited or reachable in your system
New flaws before evidence is collected
Whether attackers can reach the code
Future code changes that make it reachable

numbers.title: Will this backlog ever clear?
steps: Net burn-down: 25 − 15 = 10 a week
Time to clear: 300 / 10 = 30 weeks
To clear in 10 weeks: 300 / 10 + 15 = 45 fixes a week, nearly double the current rate
Alternative: cut arrivals by dropping unused dependencies; at 5 new a week, 300 / 20 = 15 weeks
numbers.result: Backlog plans must include the arrival rate. Removing unused dependencies is often cheaper than hiring more fixers.

india.title: NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4 on patching as maintenance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: NIST SP 800-40 Revision 4 (April 2022) defines enterprise patch management as identifying, prioritising, acquiring, installing and verifying the installation of patches, updates and upgrades. It frames patching as preventive maintenance and a normal cost of doing business, not an exceptional event. It recommends an enterprise strategy that simplifies and operationalises patching, and maintenance plans for groups of assets with similar risk, so that routine updates and emergency fixes follow known paths. The OWASP Top 10:2025 widened its former vulnerable-components category into Software Supply Chain Failures (A03).

pitfalls.trap: Sorting the backlog by CVSS score alone
pitfalls.say: Rank by exploitation evidence and exposure first, then use the score to break ties between findings that are otherwise equally urgent.

pitfalls.trap: Promising a 7-day patch SLA with monthly manual deploys
pitfalls.say: The deadline must match the delivery pipeline, so automate updates and rollouts first.

pitfalls.trap: Accepting risks with no end date
pitfalls.say: Every exception gets an owner and an expiry, and is reviewed when it lapses.

takeaways: CVSS measures severity; risk needs likelihood and context
Known exploitation and exposure decide what is urgent
Deduplicate and check reachability before scheduling work
Plan with arrival rates, and make patching routine

interactive.title: Which goes first?
interactive.prompt: Three findings arrive on Monday. You can fix one today.

choices.label: CVSS 9.8 in a test-only tool that never ships
choices.feedback: Severe in theory, but not present in production.

choices.label: CVSS 6.5, known-exploited, in the internet-facing login proxy
choices.feedback: Right: exploited and exposed beats a higher score.

choices.label: CVSS 8.1 in an internal admin tool behind single sign-on
choices.feedback: Real but less exposed; it goes on the short-deadline tier.

interactive.reveal: Exploitation evidence and exposure set urgency; the base score refines it.

seeAlso.why: Supply-chain security, where these dependencies come from
Threat modelling supplies the exposure context for triage
Audit logs help confirm whether a flaw was exploited before the patch

title: Protecting Personal Data: Minimisation and Pseudonymisation
objectives: Apply data minimisation to forms, logs and analytics
Distinguish pseudonymised data from anonymous data
Reduce re-identification risk with generalisation and retention limits

cards.title: Data you never collected cannot leak
cards.body: Minimisation means collecting, using and keeping only what a stated purpose needs. An age gate needs “over 18: yes”, not a date of birth. Delivery needs an address until the parcel arrives, not forever. Apply the same test to logs, analytics events, support exports and test databases, where copies multiply quietly. Every field you drop is one you never have to secure, disclose or delete.

cards.title: Pseudonymised is not anonymous
cards.body: Replacing names with random ids or keyed hashes is pseudonymisation. Anyone with the key, the mapping table or enough other attributes can still re-identify people, so laws such as the EU GDPR still treat it as personal data. Combinations of quasi-identifiers such as postcode, birth date and sex single out a large share of people. Anonymisation needs more: aggregate, generalise (age bands, regions), suppress small groups, or add noise. Then test that individuals cannot reasonably be singled out.

cards.title: Worked example: tokenising phone numbers for analytics
cards.body: Analysts need to count repeat callers without seeing phone numbers.
steps: At ingest, a tokenisation service swaps each phone number for a random token and keeps the mapping in a locked-down vault
Analytics tables hold only tokens, so joins and repeat counts still work
Support staff who need a real number call the vault, which checks their role and logs the lookup
Deleting a customer deletes their mapping; their tokens no longer lead to a person, though rows still link to each other
Reports publish only aggregates for groups of at least 10 people

cards.title: Misconception: hashing an email address anonymises it
cards.body: An unkeyed hash such as SHA-256 of an email address is easy to reverse. Hash a list of known addresses and match the results. It is also a stable identifier that links datasets across companies. If you need a pseudonym, use an HMAC with a secret key held in a KMS, and still treat the output as personal data. If you need no link back at all, aggregate instead.

cards.title: Trap: personal data in the copies nobody counts
cards.body: Minimisation often stops at the main database while copies spread: production data cloned into test environments, full records in logs and error reports, customer lists in spreadsheets, and analytics events carrying raw email addresses. Use synthetic or masked data for testing, log identifiers rather than personal details, and give each category a retention period so data that has served its purpose is removed automatically. How deletion reaches every store is covered in the Backend lesson on deleting data.

questions.prompt: A sign-up form must confirm users are adults. What should it store?

choices.label: The full date of birth, in case the rules change
A yes or no result of the check, and when it ran
A scan of the user’s identity document
The date of birth, encrypted in the same database

questions.explanation: The purpose needs only the outcome. A date of birth is a strong identifier, and encrypting it in the same database still keeps it. An identity scan is far more sensitive than the question needs. “In case the rules change” is exactly the reasoning minimisation rejects.

questions.prompt: An analytics table swaps names for random ids but keeps full postcode, birth date and sex. Is it anonymous?

choices.label: Yes, because no names or emails remain
Yes, provided the random ids are 128 bits or longer
No: together those fields single out many people
No, unless the table is encrypted at rest

questions.explanation: Quasi-identifiers combine to re-identify individuals, whatever the id length. Removing direct identifiers is not enough. Encryption at rest protects stolen disks, not people who can query the table, so it does not make data anonymous.

questions.prompt: Why is SHA-256 of an email address a weak pseudonym?

choices.label: Anyone can hash a list of known emails and match them
SHA-256 outputs collide too often for email addresses
The hash is longer than most email addresses
Hashes cannot be used as join keys

questions.explanation: Email addresses are guessable and widely leaked, so an unkeyed hash is reversed by lookup. SHA-256 collisions are not a practical concern, length is irrelevant, and stable hashes make excellent join keys, which is part of the danger.

questions.prompt: A postcode area has 20,000 residents aged 0 to 79. Treating a year as 365 days, how many distinct combinations of birth date and sex are possible?
assumptions: Ages 0 to 79: 80 years of birth dates
questions.explanation: Design implication: 58,400 combinations for 20,000 people is about 0.34 people each, so many residents share their combination with nobody and are unique. Five-year age bands give 16 × 2 = 32 groups of about 625 people.

questions.prompt: Order a minimisation review of a new analytics event.

items.label: Drop the fields the question does not need
Write down the question the event must answer
Swap user ids for keyed pseudonyms and set a retention period
List every field the event would carry
Coarsen what remains, such as age bands instead of birth dates

questions.explanation: The purpose comes first, because it decides what is needed. Then remove, then reduce precision, then pseudonymise and limit how long the rest is kept.

questions.prompt: A vault maps card numbers to random tokens for the rest of the system. Where does the remaining risk concentrate?

choices.label: In the analytics tables that store tokens
In the vault and the services allowed to detokenise
In the token format, which can be reversed with maths
In the link between the browser and the CDN

questions.explanation: Random tokens carry no information, so they reveal nothing without the vault. Risk concentrates where real values can be recovered, which is why the vault gets strict access control and logging. That is also why tokenisation can shrink the scope of a compliance audit.

flashcards.back: Does this purpose need this field, at this precision, for this long?
Pseudonymised data can be re-identified with a key or other attributes; it is still personal data.
Fields such as postcode, birth date and sex that single people out in combination.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-122: Protecting the Confidentiality of PII
NIST SP 800-188: De-Identifying Government Data Sets
OWASP User Privacy Protection Cheat Sheet
NIST IR 8053: De-Identification of Personal Information

mechanism.title: Privacy engineering, step by step
steps: Inventory and classify: list each personal-data field, its purpose, its sensitivity (contact, financial, health, location) and every store and processor it flows to. This data map drives everything else.
Minimise at the source: drop fields without a purpose, reduce precision (age band, city), and stop personal data entering logs and analytics events in the first place.
Separate identities from activity: tokenise or pseudonymise direct identifiers with keyed functions, and keep the mapping in a vault with its own access policy and audit log.
Control access: give people and services the least access their role needs, mask fields in support tools, and log every detokenisation or bulk export.
Limit retention: give each category a retention period tied to its purpose, and delete or aggregate automatically when it ends. Data kept past its purpose is data you did not need.
Check the result: before releasing or sharing a dataset, look for small groups and unique combinations of quasi-identifiers, and review new events and exports against the minimisation test.

useWhen: Any system holding data about identifiable people
Analytics and machine-learning pipelines that copy production data
avoidWhen: Claiming aggregated or public data needs no thought, since joins can re-identify people
Building custom anonymisation for high-risk releases without expert review

rows: Less data to protect or lose
Product pressure to collect “just in case”
Still personal data; key and mapping must be guarded
Small groups and repeated queries can leak
Less precise analysis; small groups still stand out

numbers.title: Why quasi-identifiers single people out
steps: Combinations: 80 × 365 = 29,200 birth dates; 29,200 × 2 = 58,400
People per combination: 20,000 / 58,400 ≈ 0.34, so most combinations hold nobody and many hold one person
Five-year age bands instead: 16 bands × 2 = 32 groups
People per group: 20,000 / 32 = 625
numbers.result: Replacing exact birth dates with five-year bands moves this area from about 0.34 people per combination to about 625 per group.

india.title: Guidance, research and the law
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: NIST SP 800-122 recommends minimising the collection and retention of personally identifiable information to what is strictly necessary for the purpose, and NIST SP 800-188 warns that removing direct identifiers alone may not prevent re-identification. Latanya Sweeney’s 2000 study estimated that about 87% of the US population was likely unique on five-digit ZIP code, sex and date of birth alone. Laws differ by jurisdiction: for example, the EU GDPR (Recital 26) treats pseudonymised data that can be linked back with additional information as personal data, and India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Section 8(7)) requires erasure once the specified purpose is no longer served, unless another law requires retention. Check which rules apply to your users.

pitfalls.trap: Calling hashed emails anonymous
pitfalls.say: An unkeyed hash is reversible by lookup; at best it is a pseudonym and still personal data.

pitfalls.trap: Copying production data into test environments
pitfalls.say: Use synthetic or masked data, so test systems hold no real people.

pitfalls.trap: Collecting fields in case they are useful later
pitfalls.say: Each field needs a purpose and a retention period, or we do not collect it.

takeaways: Collect only what a purpose needs, at the precision it needs
Pseudonymised data is still personal; anonymisation needs aggregation and testing
Tokenisation concentrates risk in a guarded vault
Retention limits are minimisation over time

interactive.title: What does the leaked export expose?
interactive.prompt: A support export with columns user_id, SHA-256(email), city and last order is posted publicly by mistake.

choices.label: The emails of anyone on a list the finder already has
choices.feedback: Right: hash the candidate list and match.

choices.label: Nothing personal, since the emails are hashed
choices.feedback: Unkeyed hashes of guessable values are reversible by lookup.

choices.label: Only the cities and orders
choices.feedback: The hashes link straight back to known addresses.

interactive.reveal: Minimise exports, and use keyed pseudonyms or aggregates when analysts need joins.

seeAlso.why: Keys held in a KMS protect keyed pseudonyms and tokenisation vaults
Logs are a common place personal data piles up unnoticed
Threat modelling maps the data flows a minimisation review covers
Deleting personal data across a service: cascades, tombstones and deletion workflows

title: Security Misconfiguration and Hardening
objectives: Remove insecure defaults before a system goes live
Return errors that help operators without helping attackers
Detect configuration drift continuously instead of once

cards.title: Misconfiguration is the gap between what ships and what should
cards.body: Software ships configured for an easy first run, not for the internet. Common gaps are sample apps and admin consoles left enabled, debug modes, open management ports, default accounts, storage buckets readable by anyone, directory listings and overly permissive cross-origin rules. Hardening closes the gap in three moves: remove what you do not need, change the defaults you keep, and lock down access to what remains.

cards.title: Worked example: hardening a new service before launch
cards.body: A team is about to expose a new internal tool to the internet.
steps: Start from a minimal base image or a published hardening profile, not a full general-purpose install
Turn off debug output, sample endpoints and unused services and modules
Replace default credentials and keep admin consoles on a private network behind single sign-on
Enable TLS and security headers, and review cross-origin and storage access rules
Check the configuration against the baseline in CI so a bad change fails the build
Scan running systems for drift and alert when a setting changes

cards.title: Errors should help operators, not attackers
cards.body: A stack trace, a database error with the query text, or a banner naming the framework and its version tells an attacker which exploits to try. Return a short, generic message and a correlation id to the client. Log the full detail on the server, where engineers can find it with that id. Handle unexpected exceptions in one place, so that a new code path cannot leak details by accident.

cards.title: Misconception: a hardened server stays hardened
cards.body: Configuration decays. A hotfix opens a port, someone clicks a setting in a cloud console, a new feature adds a public bucket, a package update re-enables a module. A check that passed at launch says little six months later. Keep configuration in code, review it like code, and compare live systems with the baseline continuously, so drift is caught within minutes, not at the next audit.

cards.title: Trap: hardening only production
cards.body: Attackers look for the weakest environment, not the most important one. Staging systems often hold copies of real data, test admin panels and debug modes. Preview environments get public URLs. Apply the same baseline everywhere, use synthetic data outside production, and put non-production systems behind single sign-on. A leaked staging database is still a breach.

questions.prompt: A new database appliance ships with a web admin console on port 8080 and the login admin/admin. What is the best first step?

choices.label: Change the password but leave the console reachable from anywhere
Close the console to the internet and replace the default login
Put the console behind a CDN to hide its address
Rename the admin account to something hard to guess

questions.explanation: Both problems need fixing: the default login and the exposed console. A new password alone leaves the console open to brute force and to its own flaws. A CDN still forwards requests to it. Renaming the account is obscurity, and the password is still the default.

questions.prompt: For malformed input, an API returns the database error with the query text and driver version. What is the right fix?

choices.label: Keep the details, but only for requests from the mobile app
Return 200 with an empty body so that errors look like a success
A generic error and a reference id; details go to server logs
Encrypt the error details inside the response body

questions.explanation: Clients need to know that something failed and how to report it, not how the database is built. Anyone can call the API as the mobile app does. Hiding failures as success breaks clients and monitoring. Encrypted details are still sent, and the key has to live somewhere the client can reach.

questions.prompt: A storage bucket passed the hardening review at launch. Six months later it is public. Which control would have caught this soonest?

choices.label: A yearly penetration test of the application
A stricter code review rule for application changes
Rebuilding the server images once a quarter
A continuous check of live settings against the baseline

questions.explanation: Drift happens in live systems, often through a console rather than code, so only a check of the live settings catches it quickly. A yearly test may be months late. Code review does not see console changes. Rebuilding servers does not touch a storage bucket’s policy.

questions.prompt: A fleet has 200 hosts, and each is checked against 50 baseline settings. A daily scan finds 0.5% of checks failing. How many failing settings need triage each day?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 50 a day is manageable only if failures are grouped by cause. One bad image template often explains most of them, so fix the template and redeploy.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for keeping a fleet hardened.

items.label: Scan running systems for drift and alert on changes
Pick a published hardening baseline for the platform
Check configuration against the baseline in CI before deploying
Fix the template, then redeploy rather than patching hosts by hand
Build images from it and remove unused packages and services

questions.explanation: Baseline first, then images built from it, then a gate before deploy, then drift detection in production. Fixes go back into the template, so the same drift does not return with the next host.

questions.prompt: Each pull request gets a preview environment with a public URL and a copy of production data. Security asks what to change.
constraints: Previews live for a few days

approaches.label: Same baseline as production, synthetic data, access behind single sign-on
Keep previews open but give them long, unguessable URLs
Turn on debug mode in previews so fixes are faster

rationaleOptions.label: Attackers aim for the weakest environment, not the most important one
Synthetic data removes the prize if a preview leaks
Unguessable URLs stay secret once they are shared
Debug mode is harmless in short-lived environments

rationaleConflicts.r3: URLs leak through chat, browser history, referrer headers and logs.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Debug modes can expose consoles and internals, and a few days is plenty of time for a scanner to find one.

questions.explanation: Previews need the production baseline and no real data. Single sign-on controls who reaches them without slowing reviewers down.

flashcards.back: Remove what you do not need, change the defaults you keep, lock down what remains.

flashcards.front: What to return on an error
flashcards.back: A generic message and a correlation id; full details go to server logs.
Compare live settings with the baseline continuously and alert on change.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10:2025 A02 Security Misconfiguration
NIST SP 800-123: Guide to General Server Security
OWASP Error Handling Cheat Sheet

mechanism.title: How a hardening programme works
steps: Choose a baseline: adopt a published hardening profile for each platform, such as an operating system, database, container runtime or cloud account, and write down the few deliberate exceptions and why they exist. A baseline that nobody can read will not be followed.

Build from it: produce base images and infrastructure templates that already meet the baseline, with unused packages, services, sample apps and accounts removed. Teams then start secure by default instead of hardening by hand after launch.
Gate changes: check infrastructure code and image builds against the baseline in CI, so that a public bucket, an open admin port or debug mode fails the build before it reaches production.

Shape errors and banners: route unexpected exceptions to one handler that logs detail and returns a generic message with a correlation id, and remove version banners from servers and response headers.
Detect drift: compare live settings with the baseline continuously, using cloud configuration events where available, and alert the owning team within minutes of a risky change.
Fix at the source: when drift appears, correct the template or code and redeploy. Hand-fixing one host leaves the root cause in place for the next host built from the same template.

useWhen: Any system reachable from a network, including internal and non-production ones
Cloud accounts where settings can be changed from a console
avoidWhen: Treating a one-off hardening checklist as a lasting control
Applying a baseline blindly where it breaks a documented business need; record an exception instead

rows: Anything that changed since the test

numbers.title: How much does detection speed matter?
assumptions: About 20 risky changes a year reach live systems
A daily scan runs at a fixed hour
steps: Daily scan: a change waits half a day on average, 24 / 2 = 12 hours
Yearly exposure with daily scans: 20 × 12 = 240 hours
Event-driven alerts: 20 × 5 = 100 minutes a year
These figures are illustrative; real exposure depends on how quickly someone acts on the alert
numbers.result: Moving from daily scans to event-driven checks cuts yearly exposure from about 240 hours to under 2, an illustrative estimate.

india.title: OWASP Top 10:2025 on misconfiguration
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, Security Misconfiguration moved up from fifth place in the previous edition to second. OWASP reports that 100% of the applications tested were found to have some form of misconfiguration, with an average incidence rate of 3.00% and over 719,000 occurrences of the mapped weaknesses. Its notable weaknesses include XML external entity processing (CWE-611), which has sat in this category since the 2021 edition. OWASP links the rise to the shift towards highly configurable software, which matches what teams see in cloud accounts: more settings, more defaults and more ways to drift.

pitfalls.trap: Leaving default accounts because the console is “internal”
pitfalls.say: Internal networks get breached too, so replace defaults and keep consoles behind single sign-on.

pitfalls.trap: Returning stack traces to help mobile developers debug
pitfalls.say: Return a correlation id and let developers look up the detail in the logs.

pitfalls.trap: Fixing drift by hand on the affected host
pitfalls.say: Fix the template or code and redeploy, or the drift returns with the next host.

takeaways: Defaults are built for convenience, so remove, change and lock down
Errors should carry a reference id, not internals
Check configuration in CI and continuously in production
Apply the same baseline to staging and previews

interactive.title: What does the stack trace reveal?
interactive.prompt: A service crashes on a malformed date and returns its full stack trace in the response.

choices.label: Framework versions, file paths and query shapes for planning the next attack
choices.feedback: Right: a trace is a map of the internals.

choices.label: Nothing useful, since traces show only line numbers
choices.feedback: Traces name libraries, versions, paths and often queries.

choices.label: Only which date format the server expects
choices.feedback: That is the least of what leaks.

interactive.reveal: Catch unexpected errors in one handler, log the detail and return a generic message with a correlation id.

seeAlso.why: Security groups and private subnets keep admin ports off the internet
Infrastructure as code makes the baseline reviewable and repeatable
Keeping configuration out of code makes per-environment settings explicit

title: Security Testing in the Pipeline: SAST, DAST, SCA and Fuzzing
objectives: Match each kind of security testing to the flaws it can find
Place tests in a pipeline so they block new issues without blocking all work
Recognise the flaws automated tools miss

cards.title: Four tools, four views of the code
cards.body: Static analysis (SAST) reads source code without running it and flags risky patterns such as unsanitised input reaching a query, or a hard-coded secret. It sees code paths but not runtime context, so it is noisy. Dynamic testing (DAST) attacks a running application over HTTP and finds misconfiguration and injection it can reach, but misses code it never triggers. Dependency scanning (SCA) matches your components against known vulnerabilities and licences. Fuzzing feeds large numbers of generated, malformed inputs to a parser or interface and watches for crashes and hangs.

cards.title: Worked example: placing security tests in a pipeline
cards.body: A team wants fast feedback on each change and deeper checks overnight.
steps: On each commit: secret scanning and fast static rules on the changed files, in under two minutes
On each pull request: a dependency scan that blocks known-exploited or critical reachable flaws
Nightly: full static analysis, and a dynamic scan of staging that logs in as test users of each role
Continuously: fuzzers run for hours against parsers and file-format handlers
All findings flow into one tracker, deduplicated, each with an owner

cards.title: Gate on new findings, not on the backlog
cards.body: Switch on a static analyser for an old codebase and it may report two thousand findings. If the build then fails on all of them, teams switch the tool off. Record the existing findings as a baseline, block only new high-confidence findings, and burn down the old ones as planned work. Tune or disable rules that are mostly false positives, because each false alarm teaches people to ignore the next one.

cards.title: Misconception: a clean scan means the code is secure
cards.body: Tools find patterns. They are poor at flaws that depend on meaning: user A reading user B’s invoice by changing an id, a discount that can be applied twice, or a design that trusts the client. A scan with no findings shows that the patterns the tool knows are absent from the code it reached. Threat modelling, code review and manual testing cover the rest.

cards.title: Trap: a dynamic scan that never logs in
cards.body: An unauthenticated scan of most applications tests the login page and little else. Give the scanner test accounts for each role, in a non-production environment with synthetic data, and feed it the API description so it reaches endpoints that no page links to. Check its coverage report: a scan that reached 10% of endpoints is not evidence about the other 90%.

questions.prompt: Which approach is most likely to find a crash in a custom image-format parser?

choices.label: A dependency scanner that checks known vulnerabilities
A coverage-guided fuzzer running against the parser
A static analyser with its default injection rules
A dynamic scan of the upload form’s HTTP responses

questions.explanation: A fuzzer generates many malformed files and learns which ones reach new code, which is how parser crashes are found. A dependency scanner knows only published flaws in third-party code. Injection rules do not model memory or parsing errors. A web scan sends a handful of files and sees only the response.

questions.prompt: A team switches on static analysis and it reports 1,800 findings in existing code. Builds now fail. What should they do?

choices.label: Turn the tool off until the findings are fixed
Fix all 1,800 findings before starting any new feature work
Baseline old findings; block only new high-confidence ones
Downgrade the findings to warnings that nobody reviews

questions.explanation: A baseline keeps the tool on, stops new problems from landing and leaves the backlog to be planned. Switching off loses the protection. A full freeze is rarely possible and stalls the business. Warnings that nobody reviews are the same as switching the tool off.

questions.prompt: Which flaw are automated scanners worst at finding?

choices.label: A dependency with a published remote-code-execution flaw
An API key committed to a configuration file
User A can read user B’s invoice by changing an id
A missing HSTS header on the login page

questions.explanation: Knowing that invoice 42 belongs to someone else needs an understanding of the business, which tools lack. Dependency scanners match published flaws, secret scanners match key formats, and a missing header is easy to spot in any response.

questions.prompt: A fuzzer runs 2,000 executions per second on each of 8 cores for 12 hours overnight. Roughly how many million inputs does it try?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: hundreds of millions of inputs a night is why fuzzers find edge cases that people never write tests for. Keep the corpus between runs so each night builds on the last.

questions.prompt: Order the triage of a new scanner finding.

items.label: Rate its risk using exposure and exploitability
Add a test or rule so it stays fixed
Deduplicate it against findings already tracked
Assign an owner and a due date
Confirm it is real and reachable

questions.explanation: Deduplicate first so the same issue is not worked twice. Confirm before rating, rate before scheduling, and finish with a regression check.

questions.prompt: A dependency scan flags a critical flaw in a library function your code does not call today. What is the best handling?

choices.label: Mark it not applicable and close the finding
Confirm it is unreachable, note it, upgrade on schedule
Stop all deploys until the library is removed
Patch the library’s source by hand inside your own repository

questions.explanation: Reachability lowers the urgency but not to zero, because a future change can start calling the function. Closing it as not applicable loses track of that. A deploy freeze is out of proportion for an unreachable flaw. Hand patches drift from upstream and are lost at the next upgrade.

flashcards.back: SAST reads code without running it; DAST attacks the running application.
Known vulnerabilities and licence issues in your dependencies.
Business-logic and access-control flaws that depend on meaning.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-218: Secure Software Development Framework
OWASP Web Security Testing Guide
OWASP: Fuzzing

mechanism.title: How a security testing programme fits together
steps: Start from threats: use the threat model to decide which flaws matter most for this system, such as injection in a reporting service or parsing bugs in a file converter, and pick tools that look for those flaws rather than buying everything.
Fast checks on each change: secret scanning and a small set of high-confidence static rules run on the changed files in minutes, so feedback arrives while the author still remembers the code.
Dependency checks on each merge: match the dependency list against vulnerability databases, block known-exploited or critical reachable flaws, and open upgrade requests automatically for the rest.
Deeper checks on a schedule: full static analysis, dynamic scans that log in as each role in a staging environment, and fuzzers that run for hours against parsers and protocol handlers.

One triage path: deduplicate findings from all tools into one tracker, confirm and rate each one, give it an owner and a due date, and measure the false-positive rate of each rule so noisy rules get tuned.
Human testing for what tools miss: threat-model reviews, code review of security-sensitive changes, and periodic manual testing focused on access control and business logic.

useWhen: Any team shipping code regularly, from the first release
Parsers, file handlers and protocol code, which are prime targets for fuzzing
avoidWhen: Blocking builds on noisy rules that have not been tuned
Treating a passing scan as a security sign-off

rows: Flaws in your own code and unknown flaws
Logic errors that do not crash

numbers.title: What do false positives cost?
assumptions: 200 static findings a month on new code
Tuning could cut false positives to 10%
steps: Triage time: 200 × 15 = 3,000 minutes, or 50 hours a month
False positives today: 30% of 200 is 60 findings; 60 × 15 = 900 minutes, or 15 hours
After tuning: 10% of 200 is 20 findings, so 40 fewer
Saving: 40 × 15 = 600 minutes, or 10 hours a month
numbers.result: Tuning noisy rules saves about 10 hours of triage a month in this illustrative case, and keeps people trusting the tool.

india.title: NIST’s Secure Software Development Framework
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: NIST SP 800-218, the Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) version 1.1, groups secure development into practices that any organisation can adopt. Practice PW.7 asks teams to review and analyse human-readable code to find vulnerabilities, and practice PW.8 asks them to test executable code, for example with dynamic testing and fuzzing. The framework describes outcomes, not specific products, and expects findings to feed back into fixing root causes, so that the same class of flaw becomes less likely in future work.

pitfalls.trap: Saying the scan passed, so the release is secure
pitfalls.say: Say what the tools covered and what they cannot see, then point to the manual review of access control.

pitfalls.trap: Blocking the build on a new tool’s full output
pitfalls.say: Baseline the existing findings and gate on new high-confidence ones.

pitfalls.trap: Running dynamic scans without credentials
pitfalls.say: Give the scanner test accounts for each role and check its coverage report.

takeaways: Each tool sees a different slice; combine them
Gate on new findings and tune noisy rules
Authenticated dynamic scans and fuzzing reach where others cannot
Access-control and logic flaws still need people

interactive.title: What did the scan actually test?
interactive.prompt: A dynamic scanner runs against a shop with no credentials and reports zero high findings.

choices.label: Mostly the public pages and the login form
choices.feedback: Right: without a session most of the app is unreachable.

choices.label: The whole shop, since scanners follow all links
choices.feedback: Links behind the login are invisible to it.

choices.label: All the APIs in the published API description
choices.feedback: It was not given the description, and most APIs need a token.

interactive.reveal: Check coverage before trusting a clean result. Authenticated scans with role accounts reach far more.

seeAlso.why: Dependency scanning is one part of securing the supply chain
Pipelines are where these checks run and where gates are enforced
Findings from each tool need the same triage and patch process

title: Certificates and PKI Operations
objectives: Explain what a certificate chain proves and how clients check it
Automate issuance and renewal so expiry never causes an outage
Use Certificate Transparency and CAA to control who issues for your names

cards.title: What a certificate actually promises
cards.body: A certificate is a statement signed by a certificate authority (CA): this public key belongs to these names, for this period. The names live in the Subject Alternative Name field. Clients build a chain from your leaf certificate through one or more intermediates to a root they already trust, then check each signature, the names, the validity dates and the allowed key usages. If any link fails, the connection fails.

cards.title: Worked example: automating renewal with ACME
cards.body: A team runs 300 certificates and keeps missing renewals by hand.
steps: An ACME client on each service generates a key pair and places an order for the service’s names
It proves control of each name with an HTTP or DNS challenge
It sends the certificate request to finalise the order and downloads the certificate
It installs the certificate with its intermediate chain and reloads the server
Renewal starts at two-thirds of the lifetime, and an outside monitor alerts if any certificate is within 14 days of expiry

cards.title: Revocation is weaker than it looks
cards.body: If a private key leaks, the CA can revoke the certificate, published through revocation lists or the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP). In practice many clients skip the check or treat an unreachable responder as a pass, so a revoked certificate can keep working. Short lifetimes help more: a stolen key stops being useful when the certificate expires soon anyway. Public certificate lifetimes are being cut in stages: CA/Browser Forum Ballot SC-081v3 (April 2025) set a maximum of 200 days from 15 March 2026, 100 days from 15 March 2027 and 47 days from 15 March 2029, when domain validation can be reused for only 10 days.

cards.title: Misconception: the server only needs its own certificate
cards.body: Servers must send the intermediate certificates too. Many browsers cache or fetch missing intermediates, so a broken chain often looks fine in a desktop browser and fails in API clients, mobile apps and command-line tools with “unable to get local issuer certificate”. Serve the full chain, without the root, and test with a strict client after each change.

cards.title: Trap: expiry is an outage you schedule yourself
cards.body: Every certificate carries its own failure date. Forgotten ones hide on internal services, load balancers, mTLS links and partner integrations. Keep an inventory, automate renewal, and monitor expiry from outside the system that renews. Watch Certificate Transparency logs, the public append-only logs of issued certificates, to find certificates for your domains that you did not request. A DNS CAA record lists the CAs allowed to issue for your names.

questions.prompt: Desktop browsers load your API’s docs page fine, but a partner’s backend client reports “unable to get local issuer certificate”. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The server sends its leaf certificate without the intermediate
The root certificate has been revoked by its CA
The partner’s server clock is set to a different time zone
The certificate uses an elliptic-curve key

questions.explanation: Browsers often fill in a missing intermediate; strict clients do not, so they cannot reach a trusted root. A revoked root would break browsers too. Certificate times are in UTC, so time zones do not matter, only a wrong clock. Elliptic-curve keys are widely supported.

questions.prompt: How would you find out that a CA issued a certificate for your domain that you never requested?

choices.label: Check the CA’s revocation list each day
Ask public DNS resolvers which certificates they cached
Monitor Certificate Transparency logs for your domains
Review your own servers’ TLS handshake logs

questions.explanation: Publicly trusted certificates are recorded in CT logs, which anyone can search for a domain. Revocation lists show only revoked certificates. Resolvers handle names, not certificates. An attacker would not use the rogue certificate on your servers, so your logs never see it.

questions.prompt: Why do short-lived certificates reduce dependence on revocation?

choices.label: A stolen key stops working once its certificate expires soon after
Short-lived certificates use stronger signature algorithms
Clients check revocation more often for short-lived certificates
CAs are not allowed to revoke certificates that last under 90 days

questions.explanation: With unreliable revocation checks, expiry is the dependable end of a certificate’s life, so shorter lives shrink the window for misuse. Lifetime and algorithm are unrelated. Clients do not check more often for short certificates. Short-lived certificates can still be revoked.

questions.prompt: Certificates last 90 days and renewal runs at two-thirds of the lifetime. If renewal starts failing silently right after a successful renewal, how many days until the outage?
assumptions: Renewal fails silently from then on
questions.workedAnswer: Two-thirds of 90 is 60, so the next renewal is due at day 60; 90 − 60 = 30 days of margin.
questions.explanation: Design implication: 30 days is plenty only if someone hears about the failure. Alert on failed renewals, and on any certificate within 14 days of expiry.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of an automated certificate renewal.

items.label: Prove control of each name with a challenge
Install the certificate with its intermediate chain
Generate a key pair and place an order for the names
Reload the server and check the new expiry from outside
Send the certificate request and download the certificate

questions.explanation: The order comes first, then proof of control. In ACME the certificate request is sent to finalise the order once the challenges pass. Only then is there a certificate to install, and the outside check confirms clients see the new one.

questions.prompt: What does a DNS CAA record do?

choices.label: Encrypts DNS answers between resolver and client
Lists which CAs may issue certificates for the domain
Pins the exact certificate that clients must accept
Tells browsers to use HTTPS for the domain

questions.explanation: CAs must check CAA before issuing, so it limits who can mis-issue for you. DNS encryption is a separate protocol. Certificate pinning is a client feature, not a DNS record. Forcing HTTPS is the job of HSTS.

flashcards.back: A public key to names (in the SAN) for a validity period, signed by a CA.
Strict clients cannot build a chain to a trusted root without it.
CT logs show what was issued; CAA limits which CAs may issue.

sources.title: RFC 5280: X.509 Certificate and CRL Profile
RFC 8555: Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME)
RFC 9162: Certificate Transparency Version 2.0
RFC 8659: DNS Certification Authority Authorization (CAA)
CA/Browser Forum Ballot SC-081v3: Introduce Schedule of Reducing Validity and Data Reuse Periods

mechanism.title: How certificate operations work end to end
steps: Inventory: list every certificate in use, including internal services, load balancers, mTLS links and partner endpoints, with its names, issuer, expiry date and owning team. Scanning your own address ranges and CT logs fills the gaps that spreadsheets miss.

Issue automatically: an ACME client generates a fresh key, proves control of each name with an HTTP or DNS challenge, and receives a certificate. Private CAs for internal services can use the same protocol.
Deploy the full chain: install the leaf plus its intermediates, never the root, and reload the server without dropping connections. Test with a strict client, not only a browser.
Renew early: renew at around two-thirds of the lifetime so failures leave time to react, and treat a failed renewal as an alert, not a log line.
Monitor from outside: an independent check connects to each endpoint and alerts at 30, 14 and 7 days before expiry, catching cases where renewal succeeded but the server never reloaded.
Control issuance: publish CAA records naming your CAs, watch CT logs for unexpected certificates on your domains, and have a runbook to revoke and replace a certificate quickly if its key leaks.

useWhen: Any service that terminates TLS, public or internal
Fleets where manual renewal has already caused an outage
avoidWhen: Pinning a specific leaf certificate in clients you cannot update quickly
Sharing one wildcard key across many unrelated systems, which widens the damage if it leaks

rows: Challenge setup and access to DNS or HTTP
Catches failed reloads and lost cron jobs
Alerts to triage for legitimate new certificates

numbers.title: Why manual renewal stops scaling
assumptions: Public lifetimes falling to 47 days from 15 March 2029 (CA/Browser Forum Ballot SC-081v3)
Renewal at two-thirds of the lifetime
steps: Renew at two-thirds of 47 days, which is about day 31
Renewals per certificate per year: 365 / 31 ≈ 11.8
Fleet renewals per year: 500 × 11.8 = 5,900
Per day: 5,900 / 365 ≈ 16 renewals
numbers.result: About 16 renewals every day for this illustrative fleet, which only automation can sustain.

india.title: Certificate Transparency in the RFCs
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 9162 specifies version 2.0 of Certificate Transparency. Logs are append-only Merkle trees, so that anyone can check that a log has not removed or altered entries, and domain owners can monitor them for certificates issued for their names. RFC 8659 defines the CAA record, which a CA must check before issuing, so that a domain can restrict issuance to the CAs it uses. RFC 8555 defines ACME, the protocol that most automated renewal tools speak, for both public and private CAs.

pitfalls.trap: Testing a new chain only in a desktop browser
pitfalls.say: Test with a strict client too, because browsers hide missing intermediates.

pitfalls.trap: Relying on revocation after a key leak
pitfalls.say: Revoke, but also replace the key and certificate at once, since many clients do not check.

pitfalls.trap: Monitoring expiry from the server that renews
pitfalls.say: Check from outside, so a dead renewal job or a missed reload still triggers an alert.

takeaways: Clients check the chain, names, dates and usage
Serve the intermediates, never the root
Automate renewal at two-thirds of the lifetime and monitor from outside
Use CT monitoring and CAA to control issuance

interactive.title: What happens next?
interactive.prompt: A 200-day certificate is renewed by a scheduled job on a single server. That server was retired last month.

choices.label: Nothing visible until expiry, then clients start failing together
choices.feedback: Right: the failure is silent until the deadline.

choices.label: Browsers warn users 30 days ahead and renewal moves elsewhere
choices.feedback: Browsers do not warn about upcoming expiry.

choices.label: The CA renews it, since the domain is still in use
choices.feedback: CAs issue only when asked and the challenge is passed.

interactive.reveal: Run renewal where it cannot be retired by accident, and monitor expiry from outside.

seeAlso.why: The TLS handshake is where the chain is sent and checked
mTLS adds client certificates, with the same renewal problems
Signatures are what make a certificate trustworthy
DNSSEC and CAA records, which decide who may issue certificates for a domain

title: API Security Beyond Authentication: Objects, Limits and Upstream APIs
objectives: Check access for every object an API call names, including nested and batch calls
Bound the work, and the paid side effects, one caller can trigger
Treat caller-supplied URLs and third-party API responses as untrusted input

cards.title: Authenticated is not authorised, object by object
cards.body: A valid token says who is calling, not what they may touch. The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) puts Broken Object Level Authorization first and Broken Function Level Authorization fifth. APIs make the object check easy to miss: nested routes such as /accounts/{a}/orders/{o} check the account but load the order by id alone, batch endpoints check one id out of a list, and generic lookups fetch any record by its global id. Which fields a caller may read or write is a separate check, covered in the Backend lesson on request and response fields.

cards.title: One request, unbounded work
cards.body: OWASP’s API4, Unrestricted Resource Consumption, covers requests that ask for more than the server should give: a page size of a million, a query nested twenty levels deep, a batch of 1,000 operations in one call, or an upload with no size cap. It also covers cost. An endpoint that sends a text message or calls a paid service on every request can run up a bill in minutes. Cap sizes, counts, depth and time on the server, rate-limit per caller and per operation, and set spending limits or billing alerts with paid providers.

cards.title: Worked example: hardening a nested order endpoint
cards.body: GET /accounts/{a}/orders/{o} returns one order to members of an account.
steps: Authenticate the token and identify the user
Check that this kind of user may read orders at all
Check that the user is a member of account a
Load the order where id = o and account = a, and return not found if no row matches
Apply the per-caller rate limit and a server timeout
Log denials with the caller and the requested ids, so walks through ids stand out

cards.title: Misconception: our server only fetches URLs we trust
cards.body: Webhook targets, “import from URL” fields and image links all hand your server a URL chosen by the caller. OWASP lists this as API7, Server Side Request Forgery: the request leaves from inside your network and can reach internal services and cloud metadata. Treat every caller-supplied URL as untrusted. Check the address it resolves to, not just the text, refuse redirects, and run the fetcher where its network access is limited. The SSRF lesson covers these defences in depth.

cards.title: Trap: trusting data because it came from another API
cards.body: OWASP’s API10, Unsafe Consumption of APIs, notes that developers tend to trust data from third-party APIs more than user input. If a partner or enrichment service is compromised or buggy, its responses can carry injection payloads, huge bodies or redirects to an attacker’s server. Validate upstream responses against a schema, cap their size, set timeouts, use TLS, and follow redirects only to an allowlist of known locations.

questions.prompt: GET /accounts/7/orders/991 checks that the caller is a member of account 7, then loads order 991 by its id. What is the flaw?

choices.label: Order 991 might belong to another account entirely
The account id should travel in a header, not the path
Sequential order ids leak how many orders exist
The route should check the caller’s role, not membership

questions.explanation: The membership check covers account 7, but nothing ties order 991 to account 7, so changing the order id reads any account’s order. Load the order by both ids. Moving the account id into a header changes nothing about the check. Sequential ids leak volume, a smaller issue. A role check alone still would not tie the order to the account.

questions.prompt: A customer registers a webhook URL, and your servers post events to it from inside your cloud network. Which control matters most?

choices.label: Accept only https:// URLs that use a domain name, not an IP
Reject URLs whose text contains “localhost”
Check the resolved address and send from a fenced-off network
Require the customer to be signed in to register it

questions.explanation: Checking the address the name actually resolves to, and sending from a network that cannot reach internal ranges, stops the server being aimed inward. An HTTPS URL with a domain name can still resolve to an internal host. Text checks miss other spellings and names that resolve to private addresses. The attacker is usually a signed-in customer, so sign-in does not help.

questions.prompt: GET /search accepts any limit value. An attacker sends limit=1000000. Which change fixes the root cause?

choices.label: Add a CAPTCHA to the search page in the app
Cache search results for one minute
Compress the results with gzip
Cap the limit on the server and paginate

questions.explanation: The flaw is that one request can ask for unbounded work. A CAPTCHA protects the page, not the API behind it. A cache helps only if the same query repeats. Compression shrinks the transfer but not the database and memory cost.

questions.prompt: Order ids are sequential and the API skips the ownership check. An attacker sending 50 requests per second walks through 2,000,000 ids. Roughly how many hours does that take?
questions.explanation: Design implication: an attacker can read every order in under half a day. Random ids slow guessing but do not fix the flaw. The per-object check does, and alerts on bursts of denied requests show the attempt.

questions.prompt: Your API sends customer addresses to a third-party enrichment service and stores the fields it returns in your database, then shows them on pages.
constraints: The provider is a well-known paid service
Enrichment must not block sign-up for long

approaches.label: Validate each response against a schema, cap size and time, encode on output
Trust the responses, since the provider is paid and authenticated
Store responses as returned and sanitise them once a month

rationaleOptions.label: A compromised or buggy provider can return injection payloads
Timeouts and size caps stop a slow provider tying up workers
A contract and an API key make the provider’s data safe
TLS to the provider guarantees the content is harmless

rationaleConflicts.r3: A contract does not stop the provider being breached, or attackers storing payloads in its data.
rationaleConflicts.r4: TLS protects the data in transit; it says nothing about whether the content is safe.

questions.explanation: Treat every upstream response as input: validate it, bound it, and encode it where it is used.

questions.prompt: A regular user calls DELETE /admin/users/7 directly, and it succeeds. Which API risk is this?

choices.label: Broken object level authorisation
Broken function level authorisation
Server-side request forgery
Improper inventory management

questions.explanation: The user reached an operation reserved for admins, which is a function-level failure. Object level is about which records a permitted operation may touch. SSRF makes the server fetch a URL. Inventory management is about forgotten hosts and versions.

flashcards.back: The API does not check that the caller may act on this specific object.
One request can demand unbounded work or cost; cap sizes, counts, time and spend.
Trusting third-party API responses; validate, bound and allowlist redirects.

sources.title: OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023)

OWASP API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption

OWASP API10:2023 Unsafe Consumption of APIs

mechanism.title: The checks each API request should pass
steps: Identify the caller: validate the token or key and resolve it to a user, a service or a partner. Reject requests that cannot be tied to an identity, except on endpoints deliberately left public.

Check the function: decide whether this kind of caller may use this operation at all, in one central policy rather than scattered conditions, so admin operations cannot be reached by guessing their paths.

Check every object: confirm that this caller may act on each record the request names, through ownership, tenancy or an explicit grant. Scope child lookups by their parent, check every id in a batch, and do it in the data layer where possible, so a new endpoint cannot forget it.
Bound the work: cap page sizes, body and upload sizes, batch sizes, query depth and execution time, rate-limit per caller and per costly operation, and set spending limits with paid providers.

Distrust what arrives from elsewhere: resolve and check caller-supplied URLs before fetching them, and validate, size-limit and time-limit responses from third-party APIs, following redirects only to known locations.

Know your surface: keep an inventory of every API host, version and environment, retire old versions on a schedule, and log access decisions so that walks through ids and bursts of denials are visible.

useWhen: Any API that serves more than one user, tenant or partner
APIs that fetch URLs or call third-party services on a caller’s behalf
avoidWhen: Relying on random ids as the only object-level protection
Treating a well-known provider’s responses as trusted input

rows: Child or batch lookups by id alone
Scope every lookup to what the caller may reach
Unbounded limits, batches and paid calls
Caps, timeouts, rate limits and spending limits
Resolved-address checks and a fenced-off fetcher
Schema checks, size and time limits, redirect allowlist

numbers.title: What does an uncapped limit cost?
assumptions: Each result row is about 2 KB
Ten such requests run at once
steps: One request: 1,000,000 rows at 2 KB each is about 2 GB to build in memory
Ten at once: about 20 GB, more than most API servers have
With a cap of 100: 100 rows at 2 KB each is about 200 KB per request
Ten capped requests: about 2 MB in total
numbers.result: A server-side cap turns an illustrative 20 GB memory spike into about 2 MB.

india.title: OWASP API Security Top 10, 2023 edition
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) ranks Broken Object Level Authorization as API1. API4, Unrestricted Resource Consumption, lists missing limits such as execution timeouts, upload sizes, operations per request, records per page and spending limits with third-party providers, with an example of a password-reset flow abused to send tens of thousands of paid text messages. The 2023 edition also added Server Side Request Forgery (API7) and Unsafe Consumption of APIs (API10), whose guidance is to validate data from integrated APIs, use TLS, and keep an allowlist of where they may redirect you.

pitfalls.trap: Thinking the token check covers access control
pitfalls.say: Authentication says who; each object the request names still needs its own check.

pitfalls.trap: Checking the parent in a nested route but loading the child by id
pitfalls.say: Load the child scoped by the parent, and return not found when they do not match.

pitfalls.trap: Trusting responses from a partner API
pitfalls.say: Validate them like user input, with size limits, timeouts and a redirect allowlist.

takeaways: Check function and object access on each request, every id in a batch
Cap sizes, counts, time and paid side effects
Treat caller-supplied URLs as SSRF risks
Validate what third-party APIs send back

interactive.title: What does the attacker get back?
interactive.prompt: POST /orders/lookup accepts up to 100 order ids. The handler checks that the caller owns the first id, then loads all of them.

choices.label: Every order in the list, whoever owns them
choices.feedback: Right: only one id was checked; the other 99 were loaded unchecked.

choices.label: Only the first order, since the rest fail the check
choices.feedback: The rest were never checked, so nothing failed.

choices.label: An error for the whole batch, since one id is foreign
choices.feedback: Nothing compares the other ids with the caller.

interactive.reveal: Check every id in a batch, or load the batch with a query scoped to what the caller may reach.

seeAlso.why: Object-level checks are the API form of broken access control
The full set of defences for server-side request forgery
Rate limits bound how fast one caller can consume resources
Mass assignment and over-exposed response fields, the field-level side of object authorisation

title: Parser Attacks: Unsafe Deserialisation, XXE and Decompression Bombs
objectives: Explain why native object deserialisation of untrusted data can run code
Configure parsers so documents cannot fetch files or expand without bound
Process uploaded archives with hard limits on size, count and ratio

cards.title: Deserialising can mean running code
cards.body: Many languages have a native format that rebuilds whole objects, including their types, and runs constructors or hooks while doing it. If the bytes come from an attacker, they choose which types get built. Chains of harmless-looking classes, called gadget chains, can end in file writes or command execution (CWE-502). Use data-only formats such as JSON or Protocol Buffers, and map them into explicit schemas. If a native format cannot be avoided, allowlist the permitted types and sign the payload with an HMAC so only your servers can produce it.

cards.title: XXE: the document fetches files for the attacker
cards.body: XML allows a document to define entities, and an external entity points at a URI. A request containing <!ENTITY x SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> and a reference to &x; makes a permissive parser read the file into the document, which may be echoed back. Pointing the URI at an internal address turns the parser into an SSRF tool. Nested entities can also expand a tiny document into gigabytes. The fix is parser configuration: disable DTDs, or at least external entities and entity expansion. Defaults differ between libraries and versions, so set them explicitly.

cards.title: Worked example: importing uploaded archives safely
cards.body: Customers upload zip files of documents for bulk import.
steps: Reject uploads above the size limit before reading them
Hand the job to a sandboxed worker with time and memory limits
Decompress as a stream, aborting past a total-bytes cap, a file-count cap or a 100:1 ratio
Reject entries with absolute paths or .. segments, so nothing is written outside the target folder
Parse each file with a data-only parser that has depth and size limits
Map the parsed values into an explicit schema and drop everything else

cards.title: Misconception: validating after parsing is enough
cards.body: With these attacks the damage happens during parsing: code runs while objects are rebuilt, entities fetch files while the document loads, and memory fills while an archive expands. Schema validation afterwards is still useful, but it comes too late to stop them. Protection has to be in how the parser is configured and limited before it sees a byte.

cards.title: Trap: trusting data because it came from your own system
cards.body: A serialised object read back from a cookie, a cache, a queue or a file store feels internal. But users can edit cookies, and anyone who gains write access to the cache or queue can plant a payload that your service will execute. Treat data that crosses a trust boundary as untrusted, even when your own code wrote it originally.

questions.prompt: A service stores session state as a natively serialised object in a cookie. What is the main risk?

choices.label: The cookie may exceed browser size limits
A forged cookie can make the server build objects of its choosing
Cookies with binary data are often rejected by older browsers and proxies
Users can read their own session state

questions.explanation: The attacker controls which types get built, and gadget chains can turn that into code execution. Size limits and encoding problems cause bugs, not takeovers. Reading one’s own state is a privacy issue that signing or encryption solves, but neither fixes native deserialisation of forged data.

questions.prompt: Which change best prevents XXE in an XML API?

choices.label: Escape angle brackets in the XML before parsing it
Disable DTDs and external entities in the parser
Validate the parsed document against a schema
Accept XML only over HTTPS connections

questions.explanation: XXE happens inside the parser, so the parser must refuse entities. Escaping brackets breaks valid XML. Schema validation runs after the entity was already resolved. HTTPS protects the transfer, not the server from what it receives.

questions.prompt: A 42 KB upload expands to about 5.5 GB when unzipped. Which control stops it?

choices.label: Reject uploads larger than 10 MB before unzipping
Scan the archive with antivirus software first
Unzip into a temporary folder and delete it afterwards
Stream decompression with a cap on total output bytes

questions.explanation: The danger is the expanded size, so the cap must apply to output while decompressing. A 42 KB file passes an upload limit easily. Antivirus looks for known malware, not ratios. A temporary folder still fills the disk before the clean-up runs.

questions.prompt: An import pipeline allows a 100:1 compression ratio and a hard cap of 1 GB of output. For a 5 MB upload, how many MB can it write before aborting?
assumptions: Absolute cap 1 GB, which is 1,000 MB
questions.workedAnswer: 5 MB at up to 100:1 allows 500 MB, below the 1,000 MB cap, so the ratio limit stops it first.
questions.explanation: Design implication: the ratio limit protects against small bombs, the absolute cap against large ones. You need both, and both must be checked while streaming.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of a safe import of an uploaded archive.

items.label: Parse each file with a data-only parser that has limits
Start a sandboxed worker with time and memory limits
Map parsed values into an explicit schema
Check the upload size against a limit
Decompress as a stream with byte, file-count and ratio caps

questions.explanation: Cheap checks first, then isolation, then bounded decompression and parsing. The schema step at the end keeps only the fields the import expects.

questions.prompt: A legacy service exchanges natively serialised objects with partners over a message queue.
constraints: The queue is reachable from partner networks

approaches.label: Move to a data-only format with a schema; meanwhile allowlist types and sign messages
Keep the native format and add TLS to the queue
Keep the format and filter out known gadget classes

rationaleOptions.label: A data-only format cannot build arbitrary types
Type allowlists and signatures cut risk while the migration runs
TLS stops a compromised partner from sending crafted objects
Blocking known gadget classes covers chains found in future

rationaleConflicts.r3: TLS protects the channel, but a compromised partner sends its payload through that channel.
rationaleConflicts.r4: New gadget chains are found regularly, so a denylist is out of date as soon as one appears.

questions.explanation: Remove the dangerous capability, and contain it with allowlists and signatures until the migration is done.

flashcards.back: The input picks which types are built, and gadget chains can run code.
Disable DTDs, or external entities and entity expansion, in the parser configuration.
Cap total bytes, file count and ratio while streaming.
