CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data
CWE-409: Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data

mechanism.title: How to make parsing safe
steps: Inventory parsers: list every place the system turns bytes into structures, including request bodies, uploaded files, cookies, cache entries, queue messages, configuration files and documents from partners. Each one is an entry point.

Prefer data-only formats: choose formats that describe values, not types, and map them into explicit schemas. Remove native object deserialisation wherever untrusted data can reach it, and sign anything that must round-trip through a client.

Configure parsers defensively: turn off DTDs and external entities in XML parsers, turn off type information in formats that support it, and set limits on nesting depth, string length, element count and total size.
Bound decompression: stream archives and compressed bodies with caps on output bytes, file count and compression ratio, and refuse paths that would write outside the target folder.
Isolate risky work: run file conversion and parsing of complex formats in sandboxed workers with time, memory and network limits, so a parser bug cannot reach the main service or internal addresses.
Test the parsers: fuzz them with malformed input, include known attack documents in regression tests, and track parser library versions closely, because many published flaws are in parsers.

useWhen: Services that accept files, documents or serialised data from users or partners
Systems that read cookies, caches or queues that other parties could write to
avoidWhen: Rolling your own parser for a complex format
Relying on a library’s defaults without checking them for each version

rows: Byte, count and ratio caps while streaming

numbers.title: How big can a tiny XML document get?
assumptions: Nine nested entity levels in a document under 1 KB
Level 1 holds 10 copies of a 3-byte string
Each further level repeats the one below 10 times
steps: Level 1: 10 copies of the 3-byte string, 30 bytes
Each level multiplies the copies by 10
After 9 levels: a billion copies, about 3 billion bytes or 3 GB
One more level would need about 30 GB
numbers.result: A document under 1 KB can demand about 3 GB of memory unless entity expansion is capped or DTDs are off.

india.title: CWE and OWASP on unsafe parsing
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: MITRE’s CWE-502, Deserialization of Untrusted Data, describes products that deserialise untrusted data without sufficiently verifying that the result will be valid. The OWASP Deserialization Cheat Sheet advises that the safest architecture is not to accept serialised objects from untrusted sources at all, or to accept only primitive data types. Since its 2021 edition, and again in 2025, the OWASP Top 10 has placed XML external entity processing (CWE-611) under Security Misconfiguration, reflecting that the fix is mostly parser configuration.

pitfalls.trap: Validating the document after the parser has already resolved entities
pitfalls.say: Configure the parser to refuse DTDs and external entities before it reads anything.

pitfalls.trap: Keeping native serialised objects in cookies because the data is “ours”
pitfalls.say: Users can edit cookies, so store an opaque session id or a signed, data-only token instead.

pitfalls.trap: Checking only the upload size of archives
pitfalls.say: Cap the expanded size, the file count and the ratio while decompressing.

takeaways: Native deserialisation of untrusted data can run code
XXE is fixed in parser configuration
Limit decompression by output, count and ratio
Treat data that crosses a trust boundary as untrusted

interactive.title: What does the response contain?
interactive.prompt: An XML API with a permissive parser receives a document that defines an external entity pointing at file:///etc/hostname and uses it in a field the API echoes back.

choices.label: The contents of the server’s hostname file
choices.feedback: Right: the parser resolved the entity and the API returned it.

choices.label: An error, since file paths are not valid entity values
choices.feedback: File URIs are exactly what external entities accept.

choices.label: The literal text of the entity reference
choices.feedback: That only happens when entity expansion is off.

interactive.reveal: Turn off DTDs and external entities in every XML parser, and check the settings for each library version.

seeAlso.why: Parser attacks are a cousin of injection: data treated as instructions
Uploads are the usual way archives and documents reach a parser
XXE can make the parser fetch internal URLs, which is SSRF

title: Password Reset and Account Recovery
objectives: Design reset tokens that cannot be guessed, reused or leaked
Keep recovery from revealing which accounts exist
Stop recovery from becoming a way around MFA

cards.title: Recovery is a second front door
cards.body: An account is only as strong as its weakest way back in. If a strong password and a security key can be bypassed by a reset email, a text message to a number that can be hijacked through a SIM swap, or a persuasive call to the support desk, attackers will use that path instead. Design recovery with the same care as login, and log and alert on it in the same way.

cards.title: What makes a good reset token
cards.body: Generate at least 128 bits from a cryptographically secure random generator. Store only a hash of it, with the account and an expiry of 15 to 60 minutes. Accept it once, then delete it. Send it only to a channel registered before the request, never to an address supplied in the request. Keep the reset page free of third-party scripts and set a strict Referrer-Policy, because the token sits in the URL.

cards.title: Worked example: a reset flow that resists takeover
cards.body: A user has forgotten their password and has an authenticator app enrolled.
steps: The form replies “If an account exists, we have sent a link” in similar time either way
For a real account, store a hash of a random token with a 30-minute expiry and email the link
The link page checks the token, then asks for the authenticator code, because MFA is enrolled
The new password is checked against breached-password lists
On success: delete the token, end all other sessions and notify the user on every registered channel

cards.title: Misconception: security questions add security
cards.body: Answers to “mother’s maiden name” or “first school” are often public, guessable from social media, or shared with family. They are also hard to change once leaked. NIST SP 800-63B tells verifiers not to prompt users for secrets based on this kind of personal information. Use recovery codes issued at enrolment, a second registered factor, or a verified identity check instead.

cards.title: Trap: a reset that skips MFA
cards.body: A reset link proves control of the email inbox, nothing more. If the account has MFA, the reset must still demand a second factor or a recovery code, otherwise anyone who phishes the inbox owns the account. When users have lost every factor, support-desk recovery needs strong evidence, a waiting period and notifications to the old channels, so the real owner has time to object.

questions.prompt: Which reset token design is best?

choices.label: The user id and a timestamp, encrypted with a server key
A 6-digit code sent by text message and valid for 24 hours
Random 128 bits, single use, 30-minute expiry, stored hashed
A hash of the email address and the current date

questions.explanation: Randomness makes it unguessable, single use and a short expiry limit replay, and hashing protects tokens if the database leaks. An encrypted id and time can be replayed until it expires and is not single use. Six digits for a whole day is guessable without strict attempt limits. A hash of known values can be computed by anyone.

questions.prompt: What should the reset form reply when the email address is not registered?

choices.label: An error saying that no account uses that email
A suggestion to sign up with that email instead
The same message it shows for registered emails
A CAPTCHA, followed by the account status

questions.explanation: An identical reply, in similar time, stops attackers from building lists of valid accounts. An explicit error and a sign-up suggestion both reveal that the account does not exist. A CAPTCHA slows enumeration but still reveals the status afterwards.

questions.prompt: After a successful password reset, what should happen to the account’s existing sessions?

choices.label: Keep them, so the user stays signed in on other devices
End the other sessions and notify the user
End only sessions older than 30 days
End them only if the user ticks a box

questions.explanation: A reset often follows a takeover, and the attacker may still hold a session, so it must end. Keeping sessions, ending only old ones or leaving it to a box the user may not tick all leave a live attacker signed in.

questions.prompt: A 6-digit reset code is valid for 15 minutes, and the server does not limit attempts. An attacker makes 100 guesses per second. What is their chance, in percent, of guessing it?
questions.explanation: Design implication: short codes need attempt limits, such as 5 tries before the code is cancelled. A 128-bit link token needs no such limit to stay safe.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a safe password reset.

items.label: Store a hash of a random token with an expiry
Set the new password, then end sessions and notify the user
Show the same reply whether or not the account exists
Check the token, then ask for a second factor if enrolled
Send the link to the registered email address

questions.explanation: The reply comes first and reveals nothing. The token exists only as a hash, the link goes to a registered channel, MFA still applies, and the account is cleaned up after the change.

questions.prompt: Users who have lost both their phone and their recovery codes call support to get back into their accounts.
constraints: Attackers have tried social engineering before
Real users are often stressed and in a hurry

approaches.label: Strong identity evidence, a waiting period and alerts to old channels
Ask for date of birth and postcode, then reset at once
Refuse recovery; the account is lost

rationaleOptions.label: A delay with alerts lets the real owner stop a takeover
Strong evidence resists social engineering better than facts
Date of birth and postcode prove who someone is
Refusing recovery costs the business nothing

rationaleConflicts.r3: Both are often public or leaked, so they prove very little.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Locked-out customers churn, complain and flood support.

questions.explanation: Recovery without factors is the riskiest path, so slow it down and make it loud, rather than fast and quiet.

flashcards.back: Random 128 bits, hashed at rest, single use, short expiry, registered channel only.
“If an account exists, we have sent a link”, in similar time either way.
End other sessions, keep MFA, and notify the user on all channels.

CWE-640: Weak Password Recovery Mechanism for Forgotten Password

mechanism.title: How a recovery system fits together
steps: Offer strong recovery options at enrolment: one-time recovery codes, a second registered factor such as another security key, and verified contact channels. Recovery planned in advance is far safer than recovery improvised on a support call.

Request without revealing: accept the request, reply with the same message and in similar time whether or not the account exists, and rate-limit requests per account and per source so the form cannot be used to flood someone’s inbox.

Issue a strong token: generate 128 random bits, store only a hash with the account and a short expiry, and send the link to the channel registered before the request. A new request cancels any earlier token.
Verify at use: check the token in constant time, accept it once, and if MFA is enrolled require the second factor or a recovery code before allowing a change.
Finish cleanly: set the new password after checking it against breached lists, delete the token, end all other sessions and refresh tokens, and notify the user on every registered channel.
Handle the hard cases slowly: when users have lost all factors, require strong identity evidence, add a waiting period, alert the old channels and log the case for review.

useWhen: Any system with self-service password or factor recovery
Support teams that can reset accounts on request
avoidWhen: Security questions as a recovery factor
Sending reset links to an address supplied in the request

rows: Users lose them or never save them
Phishing-resistant if it is a security key
Needs users to enrol two factors
Only as strong as the inbox
Works when all else is lost

numbers.title: How much do attempt limits matter for short codes?
assumptions: At most 10 codes requested per account per day
steps: Guesses per day: 5 × 10 = 50
Over a year: 50 × 365 = 18,250 guesses, about 1.8% of the space
Without limits, 100 guesses a second covers the whole space in under 3 hours
numbers.result: With attempt and request limits a 6-digit code holds up for a year in this illustrative case; without them it falls within hours.

india.title: OWASP and CWE on password recovery
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet recommends returning a consistent message for existing and non-existent accounts, keeping response times uniform, generating tokens with a cryptographically secure random generator, making them single use with an expiry, and not making any change to the account until a valid token is presented, so that attackers cannot lock users out. MITRE’s CWE-640 describes weak recovery mechanisms that let attackers change or recover passwords without proper verification.

pitfalls.trap: Telling users that no account exists for an email
pitfalls.say: Use one reply for both cases, so the form cannot be used to enumerate accounts.

pitfalls.trap: Letting a reset link bypass MFA
pitfalls.say: Ask for the second factor or a recovery code after the link, because the email alone is not enough.

pitfalls.trap: Leaving old sessions alive after a reset
pitfalls.say: End all other sessions and refresh tokens, and tell the user on all channels.

takeaways: Recovery is a second front door; make it as strong as login
Tokens: random, hashed, single use, short-lived
Reply identically whether or not the account exists
Keep MFA in the reset and end other sessions after it

interactive.title: Who else can see the reset token?
interactive.prompt: The reset page loads a third-party analytics script, and the token is in the page URL.

choices.label: The script can read the full URL, token included
choices.feedback: Right: page scripts can read the location, and may send it home.

choices.label: Nobody, since TLS encrypts the URL
choices.feedback: TLS protects the network hop, not code running inside the page.

choices.label: Only the analytics provider’s domain name leaks
choices.feedback: Scripts on the page see the whole URL, not just a domain.

interactive.reveal: Keep reset pages free of third-party scripts, set a strict Referrer-Policy, and expire tokens quickly and after one use.

seeAlso.why: New passwords set during a reset still need safe storage and breach checks
Recovery must not undo the protection that MFA provides
Recovery forms face the same enumeration and stuffing attacks as login

title: Least Privilege and IAM Policy Design
objectives: Scope a policy to the actions, resources and conditions a job needs
Replace standing admin access with time-limited elevation
Use last-used data to shrink permissions safely

cards.title: Least privilege, in one sentence
cards.body: Each identity, whether a person, a service or a pipeline, gets only the actions, on only the resources, for only the time it needs. The test is the blast radius: if this credential were stolen right now, what could the thief do? A key that can read one bucket prefix is an incident. A key with admin rights over the account is a disaster.

cards.title: The anatomy of a policy
cards.body: Cloud and platform policies share a shape: a principal (who), actions (what), resources (on what) and conditions (when and how), such as source network, MFA present or resource tags. In most cloud IAM systems an explicit deny overrides any allow. Wildcards are the usual mistake: “storage:*” on “*” grants deletion of every bucket. Name actions and resources explicitly, and add conditions where the platform supports them.

cards.title: Worked example: shrinking a service role
cards.body: A reporting service runs with full storage access on all buckets.
steps: Pull last-used data for the role over 90 days: it read and wrote objects under one prefix of one bucket
Write a policy allowing only object read and write on that prefix
Deploy it to staging and run the full job, watching for access-denied errors
Roll it out to production with an alert on access-denied errors
Remove the old broad policy and set a review date

cards.title: Misconception: our engineers are trusted, so admin is fine
cards.body: Trust is not the issue. Laptops are stolen, sessions are phished, tokens leak into logs and people make mistakes, such as running a delete against production instead of staging. Give engineers read access by default and time-limited elevation for changes, with approval, an expiry and logging. Keep a break-glass account for emergencies, locked away and alarmed.

cards.title: Trap: permissions only ever grow
cards.body: Access is granted quickly for a project and rarely removed. People change teams and keep old rights, services keep permissions for features that were deleted, and unused keys linger. Give grants an expiry, review access on a schedule, and remove permissions that last-used data shows have not been touched in months.

questions.prompt: A nightly job reads files from one prefix in one bucket. Which policy fits least privilege?

choices.label: Read and write on that bucket, to allow for future changes
Read on that prefix only, for the job’s own role
Read on all buckets in the account
Full storage access, limited to working hours

questions.explanation: The job needs one action on one prefix, so that is all it gets. Future needs can be granted when they arrive. Reading all buckets exposes data the job never uses. A time window does not shrink what a stolen credential can do during that window.

questions.prompt: Engineers need admin rights on the production database a few times a month. Which model is best?

choices.label: Permanent admin rights for the on-call team only
One shared admin account whose password rotates monthly
Just-in-time elevation with approval, expiry and logging
Admin rights for whoever is on call that week

questions.explanation: Elevation on demand means a stolen credential is usually not admin, and each use is approved and recorded. Permanent and weekly rights both stand open between uses. A shared account cannot show who did what, and monthly rotation leaves weeks of exposure after a leak.

questions.prompt: Which data best shows which permissions a role can safely lose?

choices.label: Last-used records for each permission over a long window
The permissions listed in the original design document
A survey asking teams which permissions they need
How many permissions it has compared with similar roles

questions.explanation: Usage data shows what the role actually does, and a long window catches monthly and quarterly jobs. Design documents go stale. Teams tend to ask to keep everything. Comparing counts says nothing about which permissions matter.

questions.prompt: An organisation has 300 service roles, and a review finds 40% grant wildcard actions on all resources. If the team tightens 15 roles a week, how many weeks will it take?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: start with the roles whose credentials are most exposed, such as pipeline and internet-facing service roles, so the riskiest half is done in the first month.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for tightening an over-privileged role.

items.label: Test it in staging and watch for denied calls
Remove the old broad policy and set a review date
Collect last-used data for the role over a long window
Roll it out with an alert on access-denied errors
Write a policy with only the used actions and resources

questions.explanation: Evidence first, then a narrow policy, then a test, then a watched rollout. The broad policy goes only once the narrow one has proved itself.

questions.prompt: An internal support tool’s role can read customer records, and its credentials could leak from a support laptop. Which policy condition most limits what a thief could do with them?

choices.label: Allow requests only from the tool’s private network
Allow requests only when they are sent over HTTPS
Allow requests only during the support team’s hours
Allow requests only when the user agent is the tool’s

questions.explanation: A network condition means a copied credential fails when it is used from the thief’s own machine. HTTPS is expected anyway and says nothing about who is sending. Office hours still leave the thief hours every day. The user agent is a header the caller chooses, so anyone can copy it.

flashcards.back: If this credential were stolen now, what could the thief do?
Principal, actions, resources and conditions; explicit deny wins.
Elevate on demand with approval, expiry and logging instead of permanent admin.

sources.title: AWS: Security best practices in IAM
Google Cloud: Use IAM securely
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls

mechanism.title: How to run least privilege as a practice
steps: Separate identities: give each service, pipeline and person its own identity rather than sharing keys, so that permissions can be scoped and every action can be traced to one owner.
Prefer short-lived credentials: use workload identity and federation so services and pipelines receive temporary credentials, rather than long-lived keys that sit in configuration and leak.
Start narrow: grant the specific actions and resources a job needs, using predefined roles where they fit and custom policies where they are too broad, with conditions such as network, MFA or tags.
Elevate on demand: give people read access by default and time-limited elevation for changes, with approval for sensitive systems, and keep a monitored break-glass account for emergencies.
Add guardrails: use organisation-level deny policies to block the most dangerous actions everywhere, such as disabling audit logs or making storage public, whatever individual roles allow.
Review continuously: use last-used data and policy analysis tools to find unused and overly broad permissions, give grants expiry dates, and remove access when people change teams or leave.

useWhen: Cloud accounts, clusters, databases and CI systems
Any credential that could leak, which means all of them
avoidWhen: Tightening production permissions without testing, which causes outages
Building one policy per person instead of roles that can be reviewed

rows: Blast radius of a stolen key

numbers.title: How much standing admin access does just-in-time remove?
assumptions: Standing admin today, around the clock
With elevation: 3 sessions a month each, 2 hours per session
steps: Standing: 24 × 365 = 8,760 hours a year, and 20 × 8,760 = 175,200 admin-hours
Just-in-time: 3 × 2 = 6 hours a month each, 6 × 12 = 72 a year, and 20 × 72 = 1,440 admin-hours
Reduction: 1,440 / 175,200 ≈ 0.8% of the original exposure
Each remaining hour is approved and logged
numbers.result: Just-in-time elevation removes about 99% of admin-hours in this illustrative team.

india.title: Cloud provider guidance on least privilege
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: AWS’s IAM best practices recommend applying least-privilege permissions, using temporary credentials for workloads, requiring MFA, and regularly reviewing and removing unused users, roles, permissions and credentials, using last-accessed information and policy generation from access activity. Google Cloud’s guidance recommends predefined or custom roles over the broad basic roles. NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 makes least privilege a control in its own right, AC-6, covering both people and processes acting on their behalf. It also asks organisations to review privileges periodically and to restrict privileged accounts to the people who need them, which is exactly what just-in-time elevation and last-used reviews put into practice.

pitfalls.trap: Granting wildcard actions to get a service working quickly
pitfalls.say: List the actions the service uses, and tighten with last-used data after a few weeks.

pitfalls.trap: Giving all engineers standing production admin
pitfalls.say: Default to read access and elevate on demand with approval, expiry and logging.

pitfalls.trap: Removing permissions in production without a test
pitfalls.say: Test in staging, roll out with an access-denied alert, then remove the old policy.

takeaways: Scope actions, resources, conditions and time
Use short-lived credentials and separate identities
Replace standing admin with just-in-time elevation
Review with last-used data and add deny guardrails

interactive.title: What can the attacker do?
interactive.prompt: A CI pipeline’s cloud key has admin rights on the account and is printed into a public build log.

choices.label: Anything the account allows, including deleting backups
choices.feedback: Right: the blast radius is the whole account.

choices.label: Only touch the pipeline’s own resources
choices.feedback: The key is admin; the pipeline’s scope is irrelevant.

choices.label: Nothing, since the key is meant only for CI
choices.feedback: Keys work for whoever holds them.

interactive.reveal: Give pipelines short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials, and block the most dangerous actions with organisation-level deny rules.

seeAlso.why: Least privilege is the design side of preventing broken access control
Secrets management decides how long a leaked credential stays useful
Workload identity replaces long-lived service keys
Roles, trust policies, federation and explicit deny in cloud IAM

title: Business Logic Abuse and Race Conditions
objectives: Spot requests that are valid but lead to outcomes the business never allowed
Make check-then-act operations atomic so one use cannot become many
Enforce workflows and prices on the server

cards.title: The request is valid; the outcome is not
cards.body: Logic flaws use features as designed, in an order or combination nobody planned for: a negative quantity that lowers the total, two discounts that stack, a refund larger than the payment, a currency switch after the price is fixed, or a confirm call made without paying. Scanners rarely find them because no single request looks malformed. Write down the invariants the business relies on, such as “the amount charged equals the server’s price minus approved discounts”, and check them on the server.

cards.title: Race conditions turn one into many
cards.body: A single-use gift card is checked with one query and marked used with another. Send 20 redeem requests at the same moment and several may pass the check before any marks it used. This is a time-of-check to time-of-use flaw (CWE-367). The fix is to make check and update one atomic step: a conditional update such as “mark used where id = X and used = false” that reports how many rows changed, a unique constraint, or a row lock inside the transaction.

cards.title: Worked example: redeeming a gift card safely
cards.body: A gift card worth 500 must be redeemable exactly once, even under parallel requests.
steps: Check that the caller may use this card
Begin a transaction
Run a conditional update that marks the card used only if it is still unused
If one row changed, add the credit in the same transaction; if none did, return “already used”
Commit, and store the result under the request’s idempotency key so retries get the same answer

cards.title: Misconception: the app enforces the workflow
cards.body: The checkout screens go cart, address, payment, confirm, but the server sees only separate requests and anyone can call them in any order. Keep the state of each order on the server and allow only valid transitions, such as “pending payment” to “paid” only after the payment provider confirms it to the server directly. A client saying “payment succeeded” is a claim, not a fact.

cards.title: Trap: trusting prices and totals from the client
cards.body: If a client sends item prices or a total, an attacker can edit them. Clients should send only item ids, quantities and codes. The server looks up prices, applies discounts according to its own rules, checks that quantities are positive and within limits, and computes the total itself. The same applies to discount percentages, shipping fees and loyalty points.

questions.prompt: A single-use voucher is checked with a SELECT, then marked used with a separate UPDATE. An attacker sends 20 requests at once. What happens?

choices.label: Several requests may pass the check before any marks it used
The database queues them, so only the first one succeeds
The web server rejects parallel requests from one user
Only the last request succeeds, overwriting the others

questions.explanation: Each request reads “unused” before the others write, so several redeem it. The database runs the two statements separately and does not know they belong together. Web servers happily handle parallel requests. Each redemption is a separate credit, so nothing is overwritten.

questions.prompt: Which change makes the voucher single-use under concurrency?

choices.label: A check in the app that the voucher still looks unused
A one-second pause between the check and the update
A conditional update that marks it used only if unused
Disabling the redeem button after one click

questions.explanation: The database applies the condition and the write as one step and reports whether a row changed, so only one request can win. A second app check has the same race. A pause widens the window. A disabled button stops double clicks, not scripts.

questions.prompt: An order becomes “paid” when the client calls /orders/{id}/confirm after leaving the payment page. What is the flaw?

choices.label: The confirm endpoint should use PUT rather than POST
The server trusts the client to say payment happened
Sequential order ids in the path can be guessed
The confirm call is missing a CSRF token

questions.explanation: Anyone can call confirm without paying. The server must learn of payment from the provider, through a verified callback or a server-side check. The HTTP method does not matter here. Guessable ids and CSRF are real issues, but fixing them still lets a user confirm their own unpaid order.

questions.prompt: The gap between check and update is 50 ms. An attacker times requests to arrive 5 ms apart. About how many redemptions can pass inside one gap?
assumptions: Each request that checks inside the gap succeeds
questions.workedAnswer: 50 / 5 = 10 requests check inside the gap, so about 10 redemptions.
questions.explanation: Design implication: shrinking the gap only lowers the count; at any gap above zero, a well-timed burst wins more than once. Only an atomic check-and-update brings it to one.

questions.prompt: A mobile app sends each cart line with its price, plus the order total, to the checkout API.
constraints: Old app versions stay in use for months

approaches.label: Client sends item ids and quantities; server computes the rest
Server checks that the total equals the sum of client prices
Sign the cart with a key inside the app

rationaleOptions.label: Prices and discounts come from data the client cannot edit
Quantity checks sit next to the price calculation
Checking the client’s sum catches edited prices
A key inside the app keeps the cart tamper-proof

rationaleConflicts.r3: An attacker edits the prices and the total together, so the sum still matches.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Anyone can extract a key shipped inside an app and sign whatever they like.

questions.explanation: Treat the client as a source of intentions, not facts: it says what it wants, and the server decides what it costs.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a race-safe voucher redemption.

items.label: If one row changed, apply the credit in the same transaction
Authenticate and check the caller may use the voucher
Commit, and store the result under the idempotency key
Mark it used only if still unused, and check how many rows changed
Begin a transaction

questions.explanation: Authorisation first, then one transaction in which the conditional update decides the winner and the credit follows. Storing the result makes retries safe.

flashcards.back: A check and the action it guards run separately, so parallel requests slip between them.
A conditional update, a unique constraint or a row lock in one transaction.
Ids, quantities and codes only; the server computes prices and totals.

sources.title: OWASP: Business logic vulnerability
OWASP WSTG: Business Logic Testing
CWE-367: Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition

mechanism.title: How to defend business logic
steps: Write down the invariants: for each money, stock or reward flow, list what must stay true, such as “a voucher credits once”, “refunds never exceed payments” and “stock never goes below zero”. These become the checks and the tests.

Compute on the server: take only intentions from clients, such as ids, quantities and codes, and derive prices, discounts, fees and totals from server data under server rules, validating ranges such as positive quantities and per-order limits.

Model workflows as state machines: store each order’s state on the server, allow only listed transitions, and move to states like “paid” only on evidence the server obtains itself, such as a verified callback from the payment provider.
Make check-and-act atomic: express single-use and limited-use rules as conditional updates, unique constraints or locks inside one transaction, and treat “zero rows changed” as the loser of the race.
Make retries safe: attach idempotency keys to operations with side effects, so a retried request returns the stored result instead of acting twice.
Test like an attacker: send requests out of order, in parallel bursts and with edited values, and monitor business metrics such as refunds per order and voucher redemptions per code.

useWhen: Payments, refunds, vouchers, rewards, stock and limits of any kind
Multi-step flows where steps happen in separate requests
avoidWhen: Relying on client-side checks or button states for limits
Fixing races with delays or retries, which only change the odds

rows: Rules duplicated in client and server drifting apart
Keys that expire before retries end

numbers.title: What does a voucher race cost?
assumptions: Each raced voucher redeems 10 times instead of once
steps: Raced vouchers: 10,000 × 0.01 = 100
Extra redemptions: 100 × 9 = 900
That is 9% on top of the face value of the whole campaign, 5,000,000
numbers.result: A race on 1% of vouchers costs an illustrative 450,000, about 9% of the campaign’s face value.

india.title: OWASP on testing business logic
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide has a whole section on business logic testing. It includes tests for forged requests, integrity checks, process timing, limits on how many times a function can be used, and circumvention of workflows. MITRE’s CWE-367 describes time-of-check to time-of-use races, where a resource is checked and then used after its state may have changed, which is the pattern behind most double-redemption bugs. Both sources stress that these flaws are specific to each application, so they need tests written from its own rules.

pitfalls.trap: Accepting prices or totals from the client
pitfalls.say: Take ids and quantities and compute prices, discounts and totals on the server.

pitfalls.trap: Checking a voucher, then marking it used in a separate query
pitfalls.say: Use one conditional update and check how many rows changed.

pitfalls.trap: Marking orders paid when the client says so
pitfalls.say: Wait for the payment provider to confirm to the server directly.

takeaways: Valid requests can produce invalid outcomes; check invariants
Make check-and-act one atomic step
Keep workflow state and transitions on the server
Clients send intentions; the server computes the facts

interactive.title: What does the order cost?
interactive.prompt: A cart accepts a quantity of -3 for an item priced 1,000, next to 1 item priced 3,500. The server multiplies and adds without checks.

choices.label: It totals 500, a discount nobody approved
The server rejects it, since prices cannot be negative
choices.feedback: The price is positive; the quantity is the problem, and nothing checks it.

choices.label: The payment provider ignores the negative line
choices.feedback: The provider sees only the final amount.

interactive.reveal: Validate quantities on the server and check invariants such as “no line can lower the total”.

seeAlso.why: Double booking is the same race, solved with constraints and locks
Idempotency keys make retried side effects safe
APIs expose business flows to the same abuse

title: Security Incident Response and Breach Handling
objectives: Preserve evidence while containing an attacker who may still be inside
Scope a compromise from logs and remove persistence, not just the first foothold
Rotate credentials and meet notification duties in a planned order

cards.title: An outage with an opponent
cards.body: An outage ends when service is restored. A security incident ends only when you know what the attacker reached, have removed every way back in, and have told the people you must tell. The attacker adapts: they may notice your response, delete logs, or use a second foothold you have not found. NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3 maps response onto the six Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions: Govern, Identify and Protect cover preparation; Detect, Respond and Recover cover the incident; lessons feed back into all of them. Speed matters, but acting before you understand the scope often tips off the attacker.

cards.title: Preserve evidence before you change things
cards.body: Rebooting, re-imaging or deleting a suspicious file destroys the evidence that answers “how did they get in and what did they take?”. Isolate a machine at the network level but keep it running, capture memory and a disk snapshot, export the relevant logs to storage the compromised accounts cannot modify, and record hashes of what you collected. Keep a timeline in one time zone (UTC) with who did what and when. Without this, you may have to assume the worst case for notification, because you cannot prove what was not accessed.

cards.title: Worked example: a cloud access key leaked in a public repository
cards.body: An alert says a long-lived access key for a deploy role was pushed to a public repository 6 hours ago.
steps: Declare an incident, name an incident lead, and open a private channel
Deactivate the key at once: the cloud’s audit logs keep its history, so nothing is lost
Export the audit logs for that key and role to write-once storage, and list every call it made since it was first used
Remove anything the key created: new users, keys, roles, functions or scheduled jobs
Rotate the secrets the role could read, check data access, and decide whom to notify

cards.title: Misconception: revoking the leaked secret ends the incident
cards.body: Attackers who get a credential usually try to keep access: they create another user or key, add a trusted SSH key, grant an app access to a mailbox, or schedule a job that calls home. Revoking the first credential leaves all of that in place. Scope the incident from the audit logs, starting at the first sighting of the attacker rather than the alert, and treat everything that identity could read as exposed until the logs show otherwise. Rotate those secrets too, because copies may already be in the attacker’s hands.

cards.title: Trap: coordinating where the attacker can listen
cards.body: If an administrator’s mailbox or chat account was compromised, the attacker may be reading the incident channel and will see you coming. When identity or messaging systems might be affected, coordinate on a separate channel whose accounts do not depend on the compromised identity provider, agreed in advance as part of the plan. Also avoid naming suspected hosts or accounts in tickets that many people can read until the attacker has been contained.

questions.prompt: A production server is found running an unknown process that sends traffic to an unfamiliar address. What is the best first move?

choices.label: Reboot it so the process stops, then read its logs afterwards
Isolate it from the network, keep it running, capture memory and disk
Re-image it from the standard build so customers are not affected
Delete the binary and watch for a few hours to see if it returns

questions.explanation: Isolation stops the harm while keeping memory and disk intact as evidence. Rebooting loses everything held in memory, often including the malware itself. Re-imaging destroys the evidence of how the attacker got in, so they can return the same way. Deleting the binary alerts the attacker and leaves any other foothold in place.

questions.prompt: After a leaked key is deactivated, the audit log shows it called “create user” and “create access key” last night. What should happen next?

choices.label: Nothing more, because the deactivated key no longer works
Turn on multi-factor sign-in for the user that owned the key
Find and remove what it created, and review all its calls
Change the administrator password and close the incident

questions.explanation: The new user and key are persistence: they still work after the original key is gone, so they must be removed and the rest of the activity checked. Multi-factor sign-in does not affect keys used by programs. Changing the administrator password leaves the attacker’s new credentials working. Deactivating the first key is necessary but is only containment.

questions.prompt: Signs suggest the attacker had access to an administrator’s email and chat account. Where should responders coordinate?

choices.label: In a new private channel on the same chat system
On a prepared channel that does not use the same sign-in
By email, with the subject line kept deliberately vague
In the usual incident channel, after resetting the password

questions.explanation: A channel independent of the compromised identity provider cannot be read with the stolen session or credentials. A new channel on the same system can be joined or read by the compromised admin account. A vague subject line does not hide the content from someone reading the mailbox. A password reset may not end existing sessions or other footholds the attacker holds.

questions.prompt: An intrusion began 200 days before it was detected, and logs are kept for 90 days. About what percentage of the intrusion window has no logs?
assumptions: Attacker first access: 200 days before detection
Logs older than 90 days are gone
questions.explanation: Design implication: when retention is shorter than a typical intrusion lasts, you cannot show what was not accessed, and notification may have to assume the worst. Keep security-relevant logs long enough to cover realistic dwell times.

questions.prompt: A build server is confirmed compromised. Evidence has been captured and the attacker’s known malware identified.

approaches.label: Rebuild from a known-good source and rotate the keys it held
Remove the known malware and keep using the server
Leave it running and watch the attacker for a few weeks

rationaleOptions.label: A rebuild removes persistence nobody has found yet
Keys the server held may already be copied, so they must change
Removing the known malware returns the server to a trusted state
Watching the attacker longer carries little risk to releases

rationaleConflicts.r3: An attacker with root may have changed anything; known malware is only what you found.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Every build signed meanwhile could carry the attacker’s changes to customers.

questions.explanation: With root on a machine that signs releases, assume anything on it could be altered and anything it held could be stolen.

questions.prompt: Order the response to a suspected leaked credential.

items.label: Preserve evidence by exporting the relevant logs
Recover, monitor closely, notify and review
Declare the incident and assign an incident lead
Eradicate by removing persistence and rotating exposed secrets
Contain by disabling the credential

questions.explanation: A named lead coordinates the rest. Disabling a credential destroys no evidence, because the audit logs keep its history, so it comes before the export. Unlike a running host, there is no memory to lose. Eradication removes what the attacker left; recovery, notification and review close the loop.

flashcards.front: First move on a compromised host
flashcards.back: Isolate it from the network but keep it running, then capture memory and disk.
Extra users, keys, grants or jobs an attacker creates so revoking one credential does not evict them.
A prepared way to coordinate that does not depend on the compromised identity or messaging systems.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations
NIST SP 800-86: Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
AWS Security Incident Response Guide

mechanism.title: How a security incident is handled
steps: Prepare before it happens: keep a written plan with roles, an out-of-band channel, contact details for legal and the people who handle regulators, log retention that covers realistic intrusion lengths, and scripts that can rotate each important secret quickly.
Detect and declare: triage the alert, and as soon as it looks real, declare an incident and name a lead. Declaring early is cheap; a late declaration loses evidence and hours.
Preserve evidence: export audit and application logs to storage the compromised identities cannot change, snapshot disks, capture memory from running hosts, and record hashes and a timeline in UTC.

Contain: cut the attacker’s access while keeping evidence, for example by isolating hosts at the network layer, disabling credentials and ending sessions. Contain all known footholds at the same moment where possible, so the attacker cannot react by moving to another.

Scope and eradicate: read the logs from the first sign of the attacker, list everything each compromised identity did and could reach, remove persistence, rotate every secret that was readable, and rebuild machines that held root-level compromise.

Recover and notify: restore from known-good sources, watch closely for the attacker’s return, decide with legal advisers whom to tell and by when (the EU GDPR expects the regulator to be told within 72 hours of becoming aware where feasible), then hold a blameless review and fund its actions.

useWhen: Any sign that an attacker or insider accessed systems or data without permission
Leaked credentials, even if nobody is known to have used them yet
avoidWhen: Treating a security incident like an outage and re-imaging first
Closing the incident when the first credential is revoked

rows: Keep the evidence that answers what happened
Rebooting or re-imaging before capturing anything
Stop further access without alerting early
Blocking one foothold while others stay open
Missing users, keys and jobs the attacker created
Return to trusted service and meet duties
Guessing the scope instead of proving it from logs

numbers.title: Why rotation has to be scripted
assumptions: The compromised role could read 120 secrets
Rotating one by hand takes about 15 minutes
A scripted rotation takes about 1 minute per secret
steps: By hand: 120 × 15 = 1,800 minutes
1,800 / 60 = 30 hours of focused work, spread over days in practice
Scripted: 120 × 1 = 120 minutes
numbers.result: In this illustrative case, scripted rotation shrinks the window in which stolen secrets still work from more than a day to about 2 hours.

india.title: NIST and AWS guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3 places incident response inside the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, so preparation, detection, response and recovery are treated as ongoing risk management rather than a one-off procedure. NIST SP 800-86 covers collecting and preserving evidence so that it remains trustworthy, including the order in which volatile data such as memory should be captured before it disappears. The AWS Security Incident Response Guide applies the same ideas to cloud accounts: keep audit logs in a separate account, prepare roles responders can assume, and practise isolating resources and rotating credentials before an incident forces you to.

pitfalls.trap: Re-imaging a compromised server straight away
pitfalls.say: Isolate it and capture memory and disk first, then rebuild from a known-good source.

pitfalls.trap: Scoping from the alert time instead of first attacker activity
pitfalls.say: Search the logs back to the first sign of the attacker and scope from there.

pitfalls.trap: Rotating only the leaked credential
pitfalls.say: Rotate every secret the compromised identity could read, and remove what it created.

takeaways: Preserve evidence before changing anything
Contain every known foothold together
Scope from logs and remove persistence
Rotation and notification need preparation in advance

interactive.title: Is the attacker out?
interactive.prompt: A leaked access key was deactivated 10 minutes after the alert. Logs show the key made 40 calls during the 3 hours before that, including creating a role.

choices.label: Not yet: the new role may still give them access
choices.feedback: Right: persistence outlives the key that created it.

choices.label: Yes: a deactivated key cannot be used again
choices.feedback: True of the key, but not of the role it created.

choices.label: Yes, provided the key’s owner changes their password
choices.feedback: Passwords do not affect access keys or roles.

interactive.reveal: Review all 40 calls, delete the role and anything else it made, and rotate what the key could read before you call it contained.

seeAlso.why: Roles, mitigation and blameless reviews from operational incident response
Audit trails supply the evidence that scopes a compromise
Secret rotation must be fast and rehearsed before an incident

title: Securing CI/CD Pipelines
objectives: Treat the pipeline as a privileged system that can reach production
Keep untrusted code away from secrets and write access
Replace stored cloud keys with short-lived, federated credentials

cards.title: The pipeline is a production administrator
cards.body: A delivery pipeline holds deploy credentials, artefact signing keys and write access to registries and repositories. Anyone who can change what the pipeline runs, whether its configuration file, a build script or a test, can act with those powers. That makes the pipeline one of the most valuable targets in an organisation. The OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks list starts with weak flow control (code reaching production without review) and includes poisoned pipeline execution, over-broad pipeline permissions and poor credential hygiene.

cards.title: Poisoned pipeline execution
cards.body: A pull request from an outside contributor can change a test so that it reads environment variables and sends them to an attacker’s server. If the job that runs that test has secrets or a token with write access, they leak the moment the build starts, before anyone reviews the change. The rule is to split by trust: jobs that run unreviewed code get no secrets and read-only tokens, and jobs that hold secrets run only code that has been reviewed and merged into a protected branch.

cards.title: Worked example: a third-party step whose tag moved
cards.body: A build job pulls in a popular third-party step to list the files a pull request changed.
steps: The workflow refers to the step by a version tag, such as v45
A tag is a movable pointer: whoever controls that repository can point it at new code
In March 2025 the tags of tj-actions/changed-files were moved to a commit that printed runner secrets into build logs
Fix: refer to the step by its full commit hash, which cannot be moved, and review each proposed update
Give the job only the token permissions it needs, so a step that turns malicious has little to steal

cards.title: Misconception: secrets are safe because logs mask them
cards.body: Pipeline platforms replace known secret values with asterisks in logs, but masking matches exact strings. Code in the job can print the secret encoded, reversed or split in two, or simply send it over the network, and masking sees nothing. Masking prevents accidents, not attacks. What protects a secret is never giving it to a job that runs code you have not reviewed, and making it short-lived, by federating the job to the cloud for credentials that expire within minutes, so a stolen copy soon stops working.

cards.title: Trap: anyone who can push can deploy
cards.body: If the deploy job runs from any branch, every person with write access, and every stolen developer token, can ship to production. Protect the main branch with required review by someone other than the author, protect the pipeline configuration files with code owners, and gate production deploys on a protected environment that only accepts the main branch and may require an approval.

questions.prompt: A public repository runs its test job on pull requests from forks, and that job has a deploy token in its environment. What is the main risk?

choices.label: The token may be printed in the public build log unless it is masked
A pull request can change a test so it sends the token elsewhere
Fork builds run against an old commit that lacks security fixes
The extra test runs use up the build minutes quota for the month

questions.explanation: Any code in the pull request runs with the token, before review, so it can exfiltrate it. Masking only hides exact strings in logs and does nothing about network calls. Fork builds run the contributor’s new code, not an old commit. Build minutes are a cost issue, not a credential leak.

questions.prompt: A workflow uses a third-party step as some-org/scan@v2, and the job holds a registry write token. Which change best stops a hijacked release of that step from stealing the token?

choices.label: Refer to the step by its full commit hash, and review updates
Refer to the step by its latest tag, so fixes arrive sooner
Turn on log masking for the registry token in that job
Run the step only after the unit tests have passed in the job

questions.explanation: A commit hash names exact code that cannot be swapped later, so a moved tag changes nothing until someone reviews an update. The latest tag pulls in whatever the tag now points at. Masking hides exact strings in logs, not network calls. Running after the tests does not change what the step’s code can do.

questions.prompt: Developers can edit the pipeline file on any branch, and the production deploy job runs from whichever branch triggered it. What fixes this?

choices.label: Ask developers to sign their commits with a personal key
Store the production credentials in a separate secrets vault
Deploy only from the protected main branch after review
Run a static analysis scan on each branch before it deploys

questions.explanation: Tying production to a reviewed, protected branch means one person cannot change the pipeline and deploy on their own. Signed commits prove who wrote a change, not that anyone reviewed it. A vault still hands the credentials to whatever job asks. A scan finds some code flaws but cannot tell a malicious deploy step from a legitimate one.

questions.prompt: A stored key is rotated every 90 days; a federated credential lasts 15 minutes. If either leaks at a random moment, its average remaining life is half its lifetime. About how many times longer does a leaked stored key stay usable?
assumptions: Average remaining life is half the lifetime
questions.workedAnswer: 90 / 2 = 45 days, and 45 × 1,440 = 64,800 minutes on average. 15 / 2 = 7.5 minutes. 64,800 / 7.5 = 8,640 times longer.
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the halving cancels out, so this is just 90 days divided by 15 minutes: 129,600 / 15 = 8,640. Short lifetimes shrink the damage window by orders of magnitude.

questions.prompt: Design the pipeline for an open-source service that accepts outside contributions and deploys to a cloud account.
constraints: Maintainers want fast feedback on every change

approaches.label: Secret-free test jobs for pull requests; deploy job only on main, in a protected environment, using federation
One job that tests and deploys, with secrets masked in logs
Maintainers deploy by hand from their laptops with an admin key

rationaleOptions.label: Unreviewed code never runs where a credential exists
Production can only be reached through reviewed code on main
Masking secrets in logs is enough to protect them
An admin key on a laptop is safer than one in a pipeline

rationaleConflicts.r3: Code in the job can send a secret over the network, which masking cannot see.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Laptops get lost and phished, and manual deploys skip review and the audit trail.

questions.explanation: Separate jobs by how much you trust the code they run, and give credentials only to the trusted side.

questions.prompt: Order a safe path from pull request to production.

items.label: Build once on main and sign the artefact with provenance
Get approval from a reviewer other than the author
Deploy that artefact from a protected environment using short-lived credentials
Build and test the pull request in a job with no secrets
Merge into the protected main branch

questions.explanation: Untrusted code is tested without secrets, a second person reviews it, and only merged code is built, signed and deployed with credentials that expire soon after.

flashcards.back: Changing code or config the pipeline runs so it acts with the pipeline’s credentials.
A signed identity token exchanged for cloud access that expires within minutes.
Jobs running unreviewed code get no secrets; jobs with secrets run only reviewed code.

mechanism.title: How to secure a delivery pipeline
steps: Map what the pipeline can reach: list every credential, token and key each job receives and what it can write to, such as registries, repositories, cloud accounts and signing services. That list is the blast radius of a pipeline compromise.

Split jobs by trust: run pull requests from contributors, and especially from forks, in jobs with read-only tokens and no secrets, and keep credentials for jobs that run reviewed code from protected branches.

Use federation instead of stored keys: have jobs exchange a signed identity token for cloud credentials that last minutes, with a trust policy that names the repository, branch and environment allowed to assume each role.

Protect what reaches production: require review by someone other than the author, protect the pipeline configuration files with code owners, deploy only from the main branch, and gate production on a protected environment.

Pin and isolate build steps: reference third-party pipeline steps by an immutable version such as a commit hash, use fresh, short-lived runners so one build cannot tamper with the next, and keep build networks from reaching internal systems they do not need.

Build once and record provenance: build the artefact once on main, sign it with provenance that says which source and pipeline produced it, and have the deploy step verify that signature before releasing.

useWhen: Any repository whose pipeline can deploy, publish or sign
Projects that accept contributions from outside the team
avoidWhen: Giving every job every secret for convenience
Long-lived cloud keys stored as pipeline variables

rows: Triggers that run fork code with base-branch secrets
Long-lived keys leaking and staying valid
Trust policies that accept any branch
Admins allowed to bypass the rules
Version tags that can be moved

numbers.title: What a stored key costs to manage
assumptions: The same cloud key is stored in 30 repositories
Updating it takes about 10 minutes per repository
Policy says rotate every quarter, 4 times a year
steps: One rotation: 30 × 10 = 300 minutes, which is 5 hours
Per year: 4 × 5 = 20 hours of rotation work
Each of the 30 copies is a separate place it can leak from
With federation there are 0 stored copies and nothing to rotate
numbers.result: In this illustrative setup, federation removes about 20 hours a year of rotation work and 30 copies of a key that could leak.

india.title: OWASP and NIST guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks project describes how attackers abuse pipelines, including insufficient flow control, poisoned pipeline execution, inadequate identity and access management, and insufficient credential hygiene. The OWASP CI/CD Security Cheat Sheet turns these into controls such as protected branches, isolated build environments and short-lived credentials. NIST SP 800-204D places these practices within software supply chain security, and the SLSA build levels describe how far a build platform goes towards producing provenance that cannot be forged.

pitfalls.trap: Running fork pull requests in jobs that hold secrets
pitfalls.say: Give those jobs no secrets and read-only tokens; run secret-holding jobs only on reviewed code.

pitfalls.trap: Trusting log masking to protect secrets
pitfalls.say: Assume any code in a job can read its secrets, and keep secrets short-lived.

pitfalls.trap: Letting any branch deploy to production
pitfalls.say: Deploy only from the protected main branch through a protected environment.

takeaways: The pipeline holds production power; protect it like production
Unreviewed code never runs next to secrets
Prefer short-lived federated credentials to stored keys
Only reviewed code on main reaches production

interactive.title: Where does the secret go?
interactive.prompt: A pull request edits a test to run a command that sends all environment variables to an outside server. The test job holds a registry write token, and log masking is on.

choices.label: The token reaches the attacker; masking only edits logs
choices.feedback: Right: the network call never touches the log.

choices.label: Masking blocks it, since the token value is recognised
choices.feedback: Masking rewrites log output only; it does not inspect network traffic.

choices.label: Nothing leaks until a maintainer approves the pull request
choices.feedback: The job ran when the pull request was opened, before review.

interactive.reveal: Give pull request jobs no secrets, so there is nothing for edited code to send.

title: Authorisation Models: RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC
objectives: Choose between role-, attribute- and relationship-based access control for a product
Recognise role explosion and combine models instead
Centralise the decision, enforce it everywhere and keep it fresh

cards.title: Three ways to answer “may this user do this?”
cards.body: Role-based access control (RBAC) grants permissions to roles and puts users in roles: “support agents may view tickets”. Attribute-based access control (ABAC), described in NIST SP 800-162, evaluates rules over attributes of the user, the resource, the action and the context: “staff may view a record if its region matches theirs and they are on shift”. Relationship-based access control (ReBAC) derives permissions from a graph of relationships: “you may edit a document if you are an editor of the folder that contains it”, the model behind many sharing systems.

cards.title: Role explosion
cards.body: RBAC is simple until roles start encoding the resource or the context. If every project needs viewer, editor and admin roles in each region, 40 projects with 3 levels make 120 roles, and 4 regions take that to 480. Nobody can review 480 roles, so people get granted broad ones instead. When role names contain ids, places or times, those parts belong in attributes or relationships, not in more roles.

cards.title: Worked example: may Priya edit document 42?
cards.body: A document app lets people share folders with teams; edit rights inherit from folders to the documents inside.
steps: The service asks the policy decision point: may user Priya perform edit on document 42?
It finds that document 42 sits in folder Finance, which is shared with team Accounts as editor
It finds that Priya is a member of team Accounts, so the relationship grants edit
It checks the attribute rule: documents under legal hold cannot be edited; this one is not
It returns allow, the service performs the edit, and the decision is logged

cards.title: Misconception: you must pick one model
cards.body: Most products mix them. Roles suit coarse job functions such as administrator or billing manager. Relationships suit per-object sharing and inheritance. Attributes suit conditions such as region, data classification, device or time. What matters more than the model is the structure: one policy decision point that answers every question with a default of deny, and enforcement points in every service and endpoint that ask it before acting, as the OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet recommends.

cards.title: Trap: deciding with stale permissions
cards.body: If roles are copied into a token that lasts an hour, a user removed from a role keeps that power until the token expires. Caches of relationships cause the same lag. For sensitive actions, check current permissions at decision time, keep tokens that carry permissions short-lived, and make revocation take effect before new sharing, so removing someone and then sharing a secret document cannot be applied in the wrong order.

questions.prompt: A file app lets users share individual files and folders with people and teams, and access granted on a folder applies to everything inside it. Which model fits best?

choices.label: RBAC, with a viewer and editor role created for every folder
Relationship-based, with sharing and folder links as a graph
Attribute-based, with each file tagged by its owner’s department
Copying the folder’s access list onto every file when shared

questions.explanation: Sharing and folder nesting are relationships, and inheritance is a walk up the graph. A role per folder causes role explosion. Department tags cannot express sharing with an individual person. Copying lists onto every file goes stale whenever a file moves or the folder’s sharing changes.

questions.prompt: Rule: support staff may view a customer’s record only if the customer is in the agent’s region and the agent is on shift. Which model expresses this most directly?

choices.label: RBAC, with one support role for each region and shift pattern
Relationship-based, linking every agent to each customer record
Attribute-based, comparing region and shift at decision time
Access lists on each record, updated when shifts change

questions.explanation: The rule compares attributes of the user, the resource and the context, which is what ABAC evaluates. Roles per region and shift multiply quickly and still cannot see the clock. Linking agents to each customer creates millions of edges that change with every rota. Updating access lists on each shift change is slow and error-prone.

questions.prompt: A user is removed from the finance-admin role but can still export reports for the next 50 minutes. What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: Roles are copied into a token that lasts an hour
The database has not yet replicated the role change
The export endpoint does not check roles at all
The browser has cached the export page for an hour

questions.explanation: A permission baked into a token lasts until the token expires, however the role changes. Database replication lag is usually seconds, not 50 minutes. If the endpoint checked no roles, access would never have stopped. A cached page does not let new export requests succeed on the server.

questions.prompt: A product needs viewer, editor and admin access for each of 40 projects in each of 4 regions. How many roles does pure RBAC need?
questions.explanation: Design implication: roles that encode resources and places grow multiplicatively. Keep 3 roles and move project and region into relationships or attributes.

questions.prompt: Twelve services each make authorisation decisions about the same users and resources.
constraints: Auditors ask why access was granted
Some services are written by different teams

approaches.label: One shared policy decision point, called by every service, deny by default
Each service writes its own checks inline in its handlers
Check permissions only at the API gateway, by URL path

rationaleOptions.label: A rule change happens in one place and applies everywhere
Each decision can be logged with the policy that made it
Inline checks stay consistent because the teams share docs
Path rules at the gateway can see which object is requested

rationaleConflicts.r3: Twelve copies of the rules drift apart however good the documents are.
rationaleConflicts.r4: A path shows the object id, not who owns it or how it is shared.

questions.explanation: Decide in one place, enforce in every service, and log each decision.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of an authorisation check.

items.label: Load the relevant roles, relationships and attributes
Authenticate the caller and build the subject
Enforce the decision and log it
Identify the action and the resource
Evaluate the policy, denying unless a rule allows

questions.explanation: You cannot decide without knowing who is asking and what for. The decision needs current data, defaults to deny, and is recorded for audit.

flashcards.back: Permissions attach to roles, and users are assigned roles.
Rules evaluate attributes of the user, resource, action and context.
Permissions follow relationships such as owner, member and parent folder.

NIST SP 800-162: Guide to Attribute Based Access Control
NIST: Role Based Access Control project

mechanism.title: How to design authorisation
steps: List the questions: write down the real decisions, such as “may this user refund this order?” or “may this team see this folder?”, and the facts each one depends on. The facts tell you which model fits.
Use roles for job functions: keep a small number of roles for broad duties, such as administrator, support agent and billing manager, and review who holds each one regularly.

Use relationships for sharing and ownership: store edges such as user member of team, team editor of folder, and folder parent of document, and derive permissions by following them, so moving a document changes its access automatically.
Use attributes for conditions: express region, data classification, time, device posture or legal hold as rules over attributes, evaluated at decision time.
Centralise the decision: put the rules behind one policy decision point, a shared library or service, so every enforcement point asks the same question the same way and the default answer is deny.

Keep decisions fresh and visible: check current data for sensitive actions, keep permission-carrying tokens short-lived, and log each decision with the inputs and policy version so you can explain it later.

useWhen: Products with sharing, teams, tenants or delegated administration
Systems where auditors ask who can access what and why
avoidWhen: Inventing a role for every resource, place or time window
Copying authorisation rules into every service by hand

rows: Coarse job functions with few roles
Role explosion when roles encode resources or context
Conditions on region, time, classification or device
Rules that are hard to review and to list who has access
Deep graphs that make checks slow without care
Needs a clear owner for the policy

numbers.title: What a relationship check costs on a list page
assumptions: Documents sit up to 6 folders deep
Each relationship lookup takes about 1 ms
A page lists 50 documents, checked one at a time
steps: One worst-case check: 6 lookups at 1 ms each is 6 ms
One page: 50 checks at 6 ms each is about 300 ms
A single query that filters the list by permission does the walk once
That brings the page cost back to a few lookups instead of 300
numbers.result: In this illustrative case, checking a 50-item list one item at a time adds about 300 ms, so relationship systems need batch or list-filtering queries.

india.title: OWASP and NIST guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet recommends enforcing least privilege, denying by default, validating permissions on every request, and preferring attribute- and relationship-based models over plain RBAC when access depends on more than a job title. NIST SP 800-162 defines ABAC, covering subject, object, operation and environment attributes and how policies combine them. NIST’s RBAC project describes the standard role model, including role hierarchies and separation-of-duty constraints that stop one person holding two conflicting roles.

pitfalls.trap: Creating a role for every project and region
pitfalls.say: Keep a few roles and move projects and regions into relationships or attributes.

pitfalls.trap: Baking permissions into long-lived tokens
pitfalls.say: Check current permissions for sensitive actions and keep such tokens short-lived.

pitfalls.trap: Scattering authorisation rules across services
pitfalls.say: Put the rules behind one policy decision point and call it everywhere.

takeaways: Roles for jobs, relationships for sharing, attributes for conditions
Role names with ids or places signal role explosion
Decide centrally, enforce everywhere, deny by default
Stale permissions are a real access bug

interactive.title: What happens to Priya’s access?
interactive.prompt: Priya is an editor of folder Finance. Document 42 is moved from folder Finance into folder Legal, which only the legal team can view.

choices.label: Priya loses edit on document 42 straight away
choices.feedback: Right: access follows the new parent folder.

choices.label: Priya keeps edit, since she had it before the move
choices.feedback: That happens only if access was copied onto the document when it was shared.

choices.label: The legal team loses access to Legal’s other files
choices.feedback: Moving one document does not change the folder’s own sharing.

Authentication and basic server-side authorisation come first
Tenant boundaries are the outermost authorisation rule
